The *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā* composed by Śrīkaṇṭha Sūri,
together with the *Ratnatrayollekhinī* commentary by Aghoraśivācārya.
Having bowed to Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness who illuminates the meaning of the Siddhāntas,
the examination of the Three Jewels is here briefly elucidated.

The Three Jewels have been defiled by some through their Vedic perspective, by others through a sense of family lineage, by others through adherence to logic, and by yet others through their own arbitrary intellects and delusion;
therefore, this correct exposition is once again offered for the ear-ornament of the wise.
Now, having been refined by the polishing of emery, I, being that very same person, make it radiant once more.
Salutation to Śiva and to Śakti, to the Bindu and to the Eternal One;
and to the Guru, to Gaṇeśa, and to the wise Kārttikeya. || 1 ||

And here, introducing the Three Jewels (*triratna*) which are to be expounded in this treatise by means of the first half-verse, he pays homage; and by the second half-verse, [he honors] the venerable Lord Śrīkaṇṭhanātha as the one who brought down all the *saṃhitās*,
Gaṇapati who removes all obstacles, and [the teacher] whose knowledge is distinguished by the hearing of the scriptures of the Siddhānta.
He pays homage to Kārttikeya for the sake of the unimpeded completion of this very work. || 1 ||

He announces those very three subjects as what is to be explained: "Having extracted from the ocean of established doctrine (siddhānta) the three known as Bindu, Śakti, and Śiva, I shall always hold them in the hearts, throats, and ears of the virtuous. (2)

Having extracted the jewels, beginning with the *bindu*, from the ocean of the Siddhānta, he has brought them forth for the virtuous to hold by hearing them with their ears, by reciting them with the organ of speech characterized as the throat, and by fixing them in their hearts. || 2 ||
Therefore, these jewels are bound together by me through the threads of my words; for that reason, the virtuous should forgive me, as the wise do not harbor malice toward a servant.

I bind [these teachings] together with threads of words; for in the world, jewels are bound with threads upon the ears and other parts of the body for the purpose of wearing them. Therefore, one should not harbor ill-will toward me while I am engaged in the worship of the True Being. || 3 ||
And because these [categories], beginning with *bindu*, share the common characteristics of jewels (*ratna*), they are designated by the word "jewel"; thus he says:

"Because they color all the principles (*tattva*s), because they are superior to passion (*rāga*) and the rest, and because they are to be maintained by the intellect of the Lords (*īśvara*) and the Śivas. (Verse 4)
And for men, by means of a mass of vast, unimpeded rays and through the provision of desired jewels, the [levels] beginning with Bindu are established in the teaching of Śiva.
Just as jewels in the world shine and manifest due to their great value, produce passion in those nearby, are held by men with their limbs, and are radiant while performing desired functions;
so too are entities such as the *bindu* and others, which exist as the material cause and the presiding agent within all the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *śakti*.

They manifest; from these causes, there is always an attachment characterized by the relationship of the gracer and the graced between the Īśvaras such as Ananta and others, and the Śivas such as the Ātman-s stationed in the levels of Sadāśiva and so forth, each according to their respective office;
and these [causes] are held by Puruṣas as objects of meditation through the intellect, possessing unimpeded and distinct splendor.

And they become bestowers of desired fruits known as worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). Therefore, the ellipsis "they too are called jewels in the Śiva-scripture" is to be supplied. Furthermore, their excellence is demonstrated by their unimpeded and unique splendor. (4–5)
The collection of reality proceeds by relying upon the Three Jewels;
for the attainment of this non-duality, it is heard in six ways from the Supreme Lord.

In that regard, the collection of pure principles (*śuddhatattva*) exists by relying upon the *bindu* as the material cause (*upādāna*), Śiva as the agent (*kartṛ*), and Śakti as the instrument (*karaṇa*) thereof, for it is impossible for an effect to arise without a material cause and the like. Furthermore, in the impure [creation], Śiva and Śakti alone are the agent and instrument through a succession [of intermediaries], while the *bindu* serves as the substrate (*ādhāra*) by way of the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti*; this we shall explain later.

In this regard, for those practitioners (*sādhakas*) who desire worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and have received the material initiation (*bhautika-dīkṣā*), the *bindu*—which has transformed into the nature of the experience of various worlds—is the goal to be attained; however, for those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*) and have received the definitive initiation (*naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā*), Śiva, inseparable from His Power (*śakti*), is the goal.
And for the sake of attaining Him, the sixfold path beginning with *kalā* is described by Śiva in the scriptures. (6)
He will establish the temporal nature (*adhvatva*) of these [categories] later; for now, he demonstrates their utility at the beginning of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth:
"This very doctrine is the threefold seed for initiation and installation.
The meaning is that since initiation and installation cannot be performed without a full understanding of this, this alone is their root.
This very point he clarifies:
"And various yogas are like obligatory and occasional ritual action. (7)
Through the realization of that [Self], the various forms of knowledge, supernatural powers, and even liberation are attained;
this alone is the supreme pinnacle known as liberation, when the individual soul is investigated.

The *yogas* are those with objects (*sālambana*) and so forth. The *nitya* [practices] consist of worship and the like; the *naimittika* [practices] consist of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like. The *jñānas* are those concerning their respective objects, as well as those concerning the bound soul (*paśu*), the fetter (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*pati*). The *siddhis* are the powers beginning with *aṇimā*. Liberation (*mokṣa*) is identity with Śiva and the attainment of the state of Sadāśiva and others. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "This liberation is of seven kinds" (Yoga 5.67).

All this is accomplished through knowledge of that. Furthermore, the attainment of this very state is the supreme limit for the individual soul; the meaning is that it is the highest liberation. || 7-8 ||
And therefore:

This should be heard through the words of a trustworthy authority, reflected upon through logical arguments, and meditated upon by those whose souls have been awakened by the descent of grace (śaktipāta) via the path of yoga. || 9 ||
Because [the descent of power] is inseparable from the ripening of impurities, those whose minds have arisen [with this realization] and are oriented toward the higher state [attain it].
By this, he indicates that for them, [this state] is established through scripture, inference, and the yogic perception of practitioners. (9)
What, then, is "authoritative statement" (āptokti) in this context? To this he says:
"In this context, authoritative statement is the established tenet (siddhānta), because Śiva alone is the possessor of authority (āptimān).
There is no one equal to those two [Śiva and his teachings] who ordains the attainment of the highest good. (10)

The word *siddhānta* (established conclusion) is well-known—through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—as referring to the ten and eighteen Tantras, such as the *Kāmika*, composed by Śiva. Therefore, the implication is that these alone are authoritative (*pramāṇa*) because they are uncontradicted. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because Śiva alone is the authoritative person (*āpta*). [Objection: But Kaṇāda, Patañjali, and others are also indeed authoritative persons; to this he replies: "No."

Regarding the phrase "by those two": it is true that they too are indeed authoritative (*āpta*) with respect to the objects within their own respective domains; however, because they are not omniscient, the scriptures composed by them cannot serve as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding objects outside their domain, such as the *bindu* and so forth. Śiva, on the other hand, is the supreme authority (*paramāpta*) because he possesses unsurpassed knowledge and action regarding all things; and thus, the scriptures composed by him [are authoritative].

Having first demonstrated that all other [scriptures] reach their goals through what is obtainable from them, [the Shaiva scriptures] are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they lead to objects not previously known and because they are non-sublated. As they say: "A valid means of knowledge is that which leads to an object not yet apprehended. Therefore, there is nothing equal to that Śiva and his scripture as a means of accomplishing the highest good (*śreyas*). Now, one might argue that the validity of the scriptures follows precisely from their eternity.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that [the Veda] is not composed by a trustworthy person; however, that is incorrect, because, like a jar or other such objects, we do not observe the production of a composition without an author. This and more has been established by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. || 10 ||

If it is argued that the Vāma and other [Tantras], being well-known as Śaiva, must also be the work of Śiva, that is not so; for they are not the work of Śiva because they propound mutually contradictory doctrines. As they say: "If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not? (See footnote 1 on page 135 of the previous section).

"Now, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them? [To this we reply: There is no contradiction, for their established doctrines are composed by other selves presided over by Śiva. He states this very point:
"The Siddhānta alone is the Siddhānta; all others are merely prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣas)."
But Śiva alone is the authoritative one; others than Śiva are considered inauspicious.
And here, "the state of Śiva" is intended to mean omniscience and omnipotence. || 11 ||
And therefore:
The established doctrine is followed by the virtuous who have been purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta);
by others, however, it is reviled out of their own willful desire, like the scriptures of the bound souls (paśu).

This very point has been stated as the sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "For those embodied beings upon whom the Power descends for the sake of non-return [to worldly existence],
their signs are an eagerness for liberation, an aversion to remaining in transmigratory existence, and devotion."

"Faith in the devotees of Śiva and in the ritual prescribed by Him" (Viṣṇusaṃhitā 5.4–5). Consequently, the Siddhānta is practiced by those who have been purified and cleansed by initiation (*dīkṣā*), which occurs immediately following the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "When one is initiated by a Guru through the intense descent of power, he becomes omniscient, just like Śiva" (Viṣṇusaṃhitā 1.21). || 12 ||
And he states by way of an illustration that there is no contradiction of its authority due to the censure of animal sacrifice:
"For the fragrance of musk is not repelled by men;
rather, it is established by reasons and is always inhaled by the fortunate. (13)

For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, those who seek these goals must possess a thorough knowledge of Śiva and the other [deities], as this knowledge is necessary for the initiation and other rites pertaining to them.

That knowledge is acquired through the study of the Siddhānta, and such study is accomplished by means of initiation, which is invariably preceded by the descent of grace (śaktipāta); thus it has been stated.

On this point, some say: by means of these unreal accounts of entities such as Śiva and the like, or by means of the exposition of the instruments for their thorough knowledge, [it is established that] according to such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1) and "The one controller, the inner self of all beings" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.12), the Supreme Self alone, whose form is consciousness, is the reality. He...

Thus, there is nothing else whatsoever that is denoted by words such as Śiva; therefore, the realization of His nature as supreme bliss exactly as it is, is the cause of liberation. To those [who hold this view], he says:
"He is propounded by the Vedāntas, by the Kula traditions, and likewise by others."
The consciousness of those deceived by bliss is permeated by bliss. || 14 ||

It is established by the Vedānta and other scriptures, such as those of the Śākta tradition, that the ultimate reality is the single entity consisting of consciousness (*cit*) and sentience (*caitanya*);

and that the very realization of this consciousness—which is endowed with bliss and whose nature is supreme bliss—is the cause of liberation. This is taught for the sake of those who are deluded regarding bliss, [in the passage]: "Bliss is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).

The meaning that the word *ānanda* found in the Śruti possesses fullness—that is, its sense of bliss—is appropriate only for those whose impurities are not yet digested and who are deluded by the error of [mistaking] it for mere pleasure; it is not so for others such as ourselves who have been graced by Śiva.
For instance, the oneness of the Self cannot be established [by them], because there are [scriptural passages] that establish multiplicity.

Because of the occurrence of scriptural texts [on plurality], because the scriptural texts on unity have other purposes, and because the observed regularity of birth, death, and so forth— which indicates multiplicity— is undeniable; and since those selves are seen to lack independence,
Śiva is the agent of their bondage, enjoyment, and liberation, while their material causes and so forth are established through both scripture and inference.

This has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*, and established by Rāmakaṇṭha and others in the *Mataṅgavṛtti* and other works; thus it should be understood from those sources. For fear of excessive length, we do not elaborate here.
Therefore, even the knowledge concerning the Self is not [fully realized] as it truly is for those who are merely attached to various scriptures.

He says that it is possible: "The profundity of the great ocean of consciousness may be discerned by the wise, provided that, having plunged into it, one does not fail to be tossed up by the waves of supreme bliss. (15)
For if the wave of delusion regarding supreme bliss, as previously described, does not toss them about,
then the wise perceive the depth of the great ocean of consciousness— the ocean of the class of Self— which consists of the nature of omniscience and omnipotence,
and possesses qualities such as eternity, pervasiveness, and manifoldness.

Furthermore, this [reality] could be determined only by plunging into it and making it an object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not otherwise; for since the authors of those various scriptures are not omniscient, this [reality] cannot be established through their words—this is the meaning. || 15 ||
But how is this known? To this he says:
"In this regard, it has been taught that [the practice] is superior to all streams;
therefore, one should perceive it with the eyes turned upward and the face directed upwards. (16)

And that nature of the Self has been declared within the stream known as Siddhānta, which is the most excellent among all the streams of scriptures such as the Vāmā; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. It establishes its superiority by virtue of being created by Śiva, stating:
"by the Lord’s right [face] and upper face. Regarding the word "declared" (*kathita*): by the word "face" (*vaktra*), the power (*śakti*) consisting of speech and protection is meant.

Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), Śiva lacks a body; therefore, [the teaching] was revealed by means of a mouth that is essentially power (*śakti*), which faces upward (*udaṅmukha*), is oriented toward bestowing grace (*anugraha*), and stands erect. The meaning is that it was manifested in the scripture produced through the sequence beginning with *nāda* from the power of the *bindu*.

[Objection: But surely, for one who is bodiless, the instruction of a scripture is impossible? [Response: That is not so, because it occurs through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), just like the creation of the world and so forth.
Because the Vidyeśvaras and others possess the capacity for understanding the scriptures. || 16 ||
Furthermore, one should examine even the reasons for that [investigation] by means of the treatises;
for in this matter, even a vast and keen intellect does not prevail without them. (17)
The intention is that even the investigation of that nature of the self must be carried out by means of the very reasons stated in the established doctrine (siddhānta). || 17 ||
Having thus established, as a digression, that the true nature of the Self is accessible only through the Siddhānta,

he elaborates upon what was stated previously— that the hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana) regarding the jewels beginning with Śiva proceed from the Siddhānta alone:
"These [jewels] are extraordinary, subtle, and concealed by Śiva."
Who knows the Three Jewels by themselves, without the established doctrine? (18)

Who, by means of their wisdom, knows both the causes—which are enemies in the blinding darkness of fallacious reasoning—and likewise Yoga, characterized as being "with seed" (sabīja) and "without seed" (abīja)? 19.

In this context, seeded yoga (sabījayoga) has Sadāśiva and other such forms as its object and pertains to the differentiated (sakala); seedless yoga (nirbīja), however, pertains to the undifferentiated (niṣkala).
By this, he also demonstrates that these [principles] are accessible through scripture (āgama), inference (anumāna), and the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of yogis. || 18–19 ||
Moreover:

Even when practiced by the virtuous, the established doctrine bestows all desires upon those whose minds are fixed on its realization, just like the wish-fulfilling gem obtained by one who possesses it. (20)

The meaning is that from the Siddhānta alone arises for practitioners the knowledge of those respective accomplished means of proof (*siddhasādhana*), and from their practice thereof comes the attainment of the fruit. || 20 ||

Having thus demonstrated the fruit of knowing the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and indicating that the purpose of this treatise is likewise that very same thing because it illuminates the subject matter denoted by that doctrine, he announces the examination of the subject matter:
"Having resorted to Him, I too have composed this [work], which rests upon Bindu, Śakti, and Śiva."
An examination is performed there; first, the drop (bindu) is investigated.
In this regard, he speaks of the accomplishment of the *bindu*:
"That from which the pure path arises, wherein it exists, and into which it dissolves—that is the *bindu* called supreme *nāda*, the cause of *nāda*, *bindu*, and the phonemes. (22)

Since the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is an effect insofar as it takes the form of the manifold universe and so forth—as will be described hereafter—it is established that its material cause (*upādāna*) is the Point (*bindu*).
Furthermore, its establishment is also due to its being the material cause of sound; thus he says: "The Point is the cause of Nāda, Bindu, and the phonemes.
In this context, what is called *nāda* is the subtle sound, which is the first manifestation of the Point and is the cause of the cognition of the objects of denotation. Through reflection...

By virtue of being devoid [of these], it is described in the venerable *Kālottara* and other scriptures. And the *bindu*—which is its effect—is like a drop of the fluid within a peacock’s egg; it is inexpressible, consisting of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa-jñāna*), and is taught in that very same work as the imperishable *bindu* (*akṣara-bindu*) due to its subtlety. Furthermore, the *arṇa* (vowel) and *varṇa* (consonant) are the gross sound (*sthūla-śabda*) produced from ether and air, perceivable by the ear. As it is said therein: "The gross is sound."
That which is subtle is said to consist of thought; that which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme. (1.8)
In that regard, in order to demonstrate that [the pure path] serves as the substratum for the worlds and so forth, he says:
"Those who have crossed the ocean of Māyā, whose great bolts of karma are shattered, yet have not reached the abode of Śiva, are the threefold Vijñānakevalas. (23)

For there are three kinds of individual souls (*paśu*): among them, those bound by *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā* are the *sakalas*; those whose *kalās* and other faculties have been withdrawn through dissolution and so forth, yet remain bound by *mala* and *karman*, are the *pralayākalas*; and those who, due to the destruction of *karman* along with the [other faculties] beginning with *vijñāna*, are bound by *mala* alone, are the *vijñānakalas*. Furthermore, through the grace of Śiva, according to the degree of the ripening of their *mala*...

Those whose great obstructions known as the impurities of karma have been shattered, yet who have not attained equality with Śiva because some residual impurity of office still remains, are the threefold *vijñānakevalins*. || 23 ||
He states what those divisions are:
"The lords of knowledge and ignorance, preceded by the Paśus, are the Sadāśivas.
Among them, the former are the Mantras and the Vidyās by name, who enjoy knowledge. (24)
Regarding that, he says "residing in the first [level], the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva)"—namely, "there, the enjoyers of knowledge" (vidyābhujas). || 24 ||
These Vidyeśvaras, who are to be commanded, number seven crores; their cities within the Vidyā-tattva are Vāma and the others, each succeeding one being higher than the last.

And their status as being commanded by the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara) is due to their performing acts of grace, while the Lords of Knowledge possess authority over the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcavidhakṛtya). || 25 ||
These nine worlds that have arisen are "expanded" by means of subtle bodies, enjoyments, sense organs, and so forth;
the meaning is that these worlds possess increasingly superior enjoyments and other qualities as one proceeds higher and higher.
Now, he says that the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are superior to these:
"The intermediate ones, whose impurities have been stilled, are the Lords of Knowledge, possessing the splendor of Śiva. (26)
Devoid of the impurity of limited authority, they have taken refuge in the reality of the Lord;
their own powers blossom through contact with the rays of the sun that is Śiva.
The state of having purified impurities, the possession of the impurity of office (*adhikāra-mala*), and being graced by Śiva are common even to the *mantras*.
This is because they are manifestations of the splendor of Śiva who performs the fivefold cosmic act (*pañcavidha-kṛtya*). As it is said in the venerable *Raurava*:
"He who effects emission, preservation, withdrawal, maintenance, and grace" (1.15). || 26–27 ||
Those eight have Ananta as their predecessor, each possessing greater qualities than the one preceding it; likewise, there are cities there for them, and Ananta is their Supreme Lord.

"Eight [are] preceded by Ananta. These are known by the names Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. Within that Īśvara-tattva, their eight worlds are exactly as before. Therefore, for these [beings], Ananta alone is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). || 28 ||
There, in those cities, were the individual souls (aṇavas), nor were there others who were their manifestations;
rather, there were others equal to Sadāśiva, who hold authority over the duties of the Lord (pati).
Furthermore, there exist individual souls who have been joined to those various worlds through the worship of the respective lords of those worlds or through initiation (*dīkṣā*).

This principle should be understood to apply to the worlds of *vidyā* as well as to the worlds of Sadāśiva and others. As it is stated in the *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*: "Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular place, he is joined to that very place."

"One becomes a possessor of accomplishment through the power of mantra" (39.2). Now he speaks of the *paśu*s and *sadāśiva*s: "In the highest [state], they are equal to Sadāśiva. (29) Having reached the summit of the path when the Supreme Lord is gracious, *Sadāśiva* here is Śiva himself in the state of office (*adhikāra*). And his states consist of office and so forth.
It has been stated that these are metaphorical: "He is an initiate, an enjoyer, and an absorbed one (layī) by way of metaphor.
However, the distinction between those such as Sadāśiva, who are to be purified, is indeed real.
Furthermore, he says that these [beings] reside in the world of Sadāśiva within the principle of Sadāśiva-tattva.
Their true essence was born, adorned with limbs, cities, enjoyments, and so forth. || 30 ||
Because they preside over Sadāśiva, they too are called Sadāśivas.
For this very reason, their bodies and so forth are merely unreal; they do not belong to that Śiva as his ultimate reality.
Thus it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara: "This form of his is traditionally taught for the sake of the practitioner's goal. (30)
He summarizes the meaning already stated:
"This path [consists] of eighteen worlds together with the enjoyers. (31)

And this path, taught as consisting of three principles, is pure and has Śiva as its agent; the meaning is that because it is an effect (*kārya*), it has Śiva as its agent. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that the worlds of Nivṛtti and the other kalās, as well as the principles of Śakti and Śiva, are included within the principle of Sadāśiva alone. || 31 ||
Since this pure path (śuddhādhvan) is an effect, it must have some eternal cause; and that [cause] is called Bindu. Thus he says:
"The multitude of principles beginning with Sadāśiva has an eternal material cause. (32)
Because it is subject to modification, just like a jar, so too is this [universe];
therefore, this path beginning with Sadāśiva is also subject to modification, and consequently, it does not have an eternal material cause. || 32 ||

But is it not the case that, since the lump of clay—the material cause of a jar—is impermanent, this [proposed] material cause of the pure path must also be impermanent? Thus, because it establishes a property contrary to the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), is this reason "because of being subject to modification" (*vikāritvāt*) not contradictory (*viruddha*)? To this, he says:
Even the earthen jar would have the illusory [consciousness] as its material cause. || 33 ||
Even though the jar has clay as its direct material cause, Māyā alone is its ultimate material cause through a causal chain. || 33 ||
Why is this so? He says:
"Because they possess destruction and origination, and likewise because of their being subject to transformation.
The intended meaning is as follows: for things that possess the nature of origination and destruction...

Even though there exists a relationship of intermediate cause and effect in the form of subordinate transformations such as the jar and its shards, one must nevertheless accept that the eternal supreme cause called *māyā* is the ultimate material source (*upādāna*) for the principles (*tattvas*) such as earth through a continuous succession;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And it is stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "The *māyā*-principle..."
"The seed of the world is indestructible and of an imperishable nature."
He establishes this very point through elaboration: "Whatever entity is produced, that is an illusion, just like a magical creation (kalā). (34)
The Great Lord has stated that arising and destruction are illusory properties;
the sense is that this is established even by the words of a reliable authority.

Now, in order to demonstrate that according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), it is Māyā itself—which undergoes the designations of "origination" and "destruction" through the distinctions of states such as Kalā—that transforms by means of its effects beginning with Kalā, he states the meaning of the word "transformation" (pariṇāma): "For the transformation of entities consists in the relinquishing of their prior state. (35)
The attainment of another state is like milk becoming curd, and curd becoming whey; therein, the state of whey is defined. (36)
In order to define the nature of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he says: "Therein" (vv. 35–36).
For it is thus:
neither from curd nor from milk [is it produced], since those two are considered to be in their prior states;
the meaning is that in the state of curd or in the state of milk, the state of buttermilk does not exist. For instance:
Milk itself transforms into the form of curds and so forth; furthermore, we observe such designations as "the milk has perished" and "the curds have arisen.
This very point he states:
For a single entity exists in six states; first it is milk, and then it becomes curd. (37)

The meaning is that because the production of what is non-existent is impossible, curd is merely manifested from milk which already exists, and buttermilk is merely manifested from curd which already exists. Furthermore, this doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been demonstrated by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*. || 37 ||

Just as milk alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of effects such as curds and butter— which possess diverse causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) due to the differences in their states and transformations— so too is Māyā alone [the cause] of the effects beginning with *kalā*, which possess diverse transformations through the distinctions of the *tattvas* and worlds, and which likewise possess diverse causal efficiencies, whether directly or indirectly.
He states that it is the ultimate cause:
"Subsequently, *takra* (buttermilk) and likewise *māyā*, through their manifold transformations, are the imperishable material causes (*upādāna*) of both real and unreal entities. (38)

If it is argued that, like milk, Māyā is impermanent because it undergoes transformation (pariṇāma) by way of its own essence, that is not so; for in every respect the example is untenable, as this example applies only to the mere fact of being subject to transformation. Consequently, there is no fault, since Māyā transforms only in one part, according to the analogy of the ghee-insect. || 38 ||

Having thus established that even a jar possesses an eternal material cause through a lineage [of causes], he concludes: "Therefore, the illustration is sound, possessing the aforementioned qualification.
That is to say, it is such that its qualification—consisting in the nature of having an eternal material cause—is excellently established and stated.
He states the proof of the *bindu* by means of an inference by elimination (*pāriśeṣikānumāna*):
"It is neither Māyā, nor Īśvara, nor Aṇu, nor Śakti, because it belongs to the Pure Path (*śuddhavartman*). (39)
Therefore, the *bindu* is obtained by means of what remains as the material cause (*upādāna*).
In this regard, he establishes that *māyā* is not the material cause:
"For instance, that *māyā* of theirs was agitated by Anantatejas. (40)
She gave birth to the entire collection of principles (tattvas), beginning with water and ending with the earth.

Among these, that which is Māyā, being insentient, produces its own effects only when agitated by the infinite power [of Śiva]. As it is said in the venerable Kiraṇa-tantra: "In the pure path, Śiva is declared to be the agent; Ananta [is the agent] in the impure."
"The Lord" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.27). || 40 ||
In that very context, he states the reasons:
"Because of being impure and insentient, and likewise because of being a path of illusion. (41)

Because it is accompanied by suffering through the succession of the impurities of *māyīya*, *kārmāṇava*, and *āṇava*; and because it is to be experienced by all individual souls (*sakalāṇu*) through the arising of transformations as well. (42)

Since this impure path (aśuddhādhvan) is impure, it possesses insentience; since it is the path of Māyā, it is the cause of delusion; since it is accompanied by suffering; and since it is characterized by the impurities of Māyā—such as the conceit of self in what is not-self—and by the Kārma [impurity], which is the cause of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

The connection of the individual soul (*aṇu*) with the *āṇava* impurity—which consists of the causal conditions such as error (*viparyaya*), attachment (*āsakti*), and so forth, and which is an eternal obscuration known as "bondage" (*paśutva*)—is established because [this impurity] alone generates the body, senses, and other faculties for those who possess the three bonds. For this very reason, it is through the worlds and other means that [the impurity] serves as the object of enjoyment for all individual souls; and because it is the means for experiencing the fruits of various karmas, it is manifold.

There are manifold arisings and increases of transformation; therefore, Māyā, agitated by the Infinite (Śiva), produces such an effect, because it is impossible for the pure Śiva to possess agency with respect to an impure object. If this is so, does it not follow that Śiva is not the agent of everything? No, for what is denied here is direct agency (*sākṣāt-kartṛtva*), and not the status of being an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*).
For even Ananta and the others cannot function as agents without being presided over by Him. || 41-42 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"Because Māyā is pervasive within the insentient, possesses transformation, and, in the production of the kalās and so forth, is endowed with a body and other such attributes. (43)
It will undoubtedly lead the person who is dependent on another, just as gold leads the smith in the work of producing a crown. 44.

If this is so, does it not follow that even Śiva, by virtue of being an agent within the pure realm (*śuddhaviṣaya*), must possess a body, sense organs, and so forth? No, for he is endowed with eternal, stainless, and unsurpassed knowledge and action regarding all objects; moreover, we observe that even a soul devoid of a body can be an agent in such acts as the movement of its own [subtle] body. However, there is no contradiction in the case of Ananta, who requires a body and the like due to his connection with the impurity of office (*adhikāramala*). (43–44)
And for this reason:
although she is indeed the very object of conceptual cognition, she is agitated by the Infinite Lord, just as clay is by a potter. (45)
The sense is that agency is observed in embodied beings only with respect to objects of conceptual cognition. || 45 ||
To explain why this is so, he says:
"Conceptual cognition [is attributed] to consciousness because of its permeation by words.
Because of the very mention of words in the form of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), such as "this is a jar," which consists of conceptual cognition, the mind is perceived.
What follows from this? To this he says:
"But that sound is fourfold, through the divisions of speech (vāk) beginning with vaikharī. (46)
It arises from the agitation of the *bindu* for the purpose of perceiving the object of Ananta.

For the arising of conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) regarding Ananta, sound (*śabda*) is necessarily required. At that time, however, because the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) has not yet arisen, it is not possible for sound to be manifested by gross space (*sthūlākāśa*).
It must be accepted that sound is produced solely from the *bindu* agitated by Śiva; and he will describe its four functions, beginning with *vaikharī*.
In this regard, the existence of *bindu* is established also by virtue of its being the material cause (*upādāna*) of sound. || 46 ||
Furthermore:
The Lord Ananta, whose body is knowledge, is considered the agitator. || 47 ||
And that [power] of Māyā is called the *bindu-tattva* by the learned.
The connection of Ananta with a *bindu*-body is heard in scripture; the sense is that the *bindu* is established as its material cause (*upādāna*).
The conclusion here is:
Therefore, Māyā is not the material cause; likewise, this Maheśvara [is not so]. (48)
The meaning is that here, in the pure path (śuddhādhvan), the *bindu* alone is the material cause (*upādāna*). What is the use of this postulated *bindu*, which is not well-known?

Let it be that Īśvara, or his power (*śakti*), is the material cause in the pure path. To this he replies: "In the same way, this [is the cause]," because of its consciousness, its non-modification, and its transformation; therefore, it is so.
The Self and Śakti are to be known; their detailed exposition will be explained right here. || 49 ||
For it is observed that material causes such as clay are insentient, whereas the powers of Śiva and the Self are sentient;

therefore, they cannot be the material cause. Furthermore, a material cause produces an effect either through transformation (*pariṇāma*), as milk becomes curd, or through a change of state (*vṛtti*), as a cloth takes on the form of a house and so forth.

However, for these [entities] beginning with Śiva, modification (*vṛtti*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) are not possible, because they are changeless; for if they were subject to change, it would entail defects such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and non-eternality (*anityatva*). An elaboration on this will occur right here [later]. And this has been stated by us in the *Tattvaprakāśavṛtti*. (49)
Otherwise, he states the proof for the existence of the *bindu*:
"From this also, the *bindu* is perceived, because of the observation of the inequality of atoms.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the observation of the inequality of atoms (*aṇuvaiṣamyadarśanāt*). [This refers to] the atoms, which are the selves (*ātman*).
Because of the observation of differences in knowledge and so forth.
He states the very inequality:
"Some individuals are seen to be endowed with little knowledge and little activity. (50)
But others beyond them are even more superior, being omniscient and endowed with power.
He states that this diversity among them does not arise from themselves:
"The *pudgala* is considered conscious, eternal, and devoid of transformation. (51)

For the self is established by its own self-awareness as the synthesizer of the cognitions that determine infinite jars, cloths, and so forth at all times; and because it is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma belonging to other bodies, its consciousness and eternity are established.
Thus, it is heard in the scriptures that no modification of this [self] is possible. || 51 ||
For otherwise, if it were subject to modification, it would be insentient and non-eternal, like a jar or a wall.
And this same logic applies equally to power (*śakti*), because there is no distinction between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmin*); thus he says:
In the same way, consciousness is the power belonging to those two as well, even though they are unchanging.
And this has already been demonstrated. It is said in the *Nādakārikās*:

"The Self is here declared to be unchangeable, and its power likewise; therefore, those two are not capable of existing in manifold ways, because they would otherwise be subject to modification in the absence of consciousness" (verse 19). For this very reason, he states that the diversity of those two is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*)—namely, "of those two also... (verse 52).
That which exists in manifold ways must arise through the power of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
and therefore—when the atomic consciousness perceives objects such as *māyā* and the like, it becomes conjoined with them. (53)
And that Bindu, which possesses manifold functions due to its various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
is that by which the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the selves— conjoined with Nāda as its transformed state, which is the seed of the intellect (*buddhi*) for the purpose of denotation—
proceeds toward the perception of objects associated with Māyā and conceptualization; and of which...
That which, endowed with various differentiated modes of activity known as *nāda* that are individually determined for each soul, shines forth in manifold ways, is the *bindu*.

This has been explained in detail by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha in his *Nādakārikās*. And it is stated in the illustrious *Kālottara*: "That supreme seed called *nāda* resides within all beings" (1.5). || 53 ||
[Objection: Might there not be a variety of knowledge and so forth among individual selves, just as there is a variety of experiences, due solely to karma which is determined for each self?
To this he says:
"The variety of the atom [the self] does not arise through karma alone, without dependence [on something else]. (54)
The diversity of experience also occurs only through that [agent] acting in dependence [on other factors];

for it is karma, indeed, which—depending upon the principles (tattvas) such as Kalā and the worlds (bhuvanas) and so forth—produces the variety of experiences. Otherwise, even the elements such as earth would be of no use. || 54 ||
In this way, even the variety of cognitions acts only when accompanied by *nāda*, and not alone. He demonstrates that very state of dependence:
"Sandalwood and other things produce a variety of experiences of action. (55)
If that [consciousness] itself were to perform that [action], then what would be the use of those [auxiliaries]? Let them be discarded.
The point is this: action alone produces the fruit, while its diversity arises solely from the diversity of its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Now, one might object: "From karma come various bodies, objects, and instruments" (this is the reading found in that [text]).
"Of embodied beings" (*śarīriṇām*), according to the venerable *Svāyambhuva-śruti* (32.13), it is action alone that produces the diversity of means as well.
True; there is no contradiction, for it is precisely through the diversity of means that action produces the diversity of results, and not by itself alone. || 55 ||
This very point is confirmed: "The activity of all beings has its cause in rejection and acquisition. (56)

For it is only when the reality of the objects of dependence exists that the activity of beings toward the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the acquisition of what is to be adopted is possible; not otherwise. 56.
He states the proof of the *bindu* by another method:

"Furthermore, they declare that [the *bindu*] to be the unsurpassed, imperishable ether (*ākāśa*) for those Śivas who possess unequalled sovereignty over both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and creative authority (*adhikāra*). (57)
Just as space is the cause of the hosts of luminaries, being the primal cause of the elements and so forth—

just as space, which is composed of the five elements and the rest, serves as the cause for the enjoyment and the functional capacity of the sun and other luminaries by providing them with room and by manifesting gross sound— in the same way...

Bindu is established as the cause of both experience (*bhoga*) and authority (*adhikāra*) by providing space and generating sound for the Śivas residing in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*)— namely, the Vidyeśvaras and others who possess the nature of Śiva consisting of omniscience and omnipotence. Those learned in the Āgamas know it as the supreme void (*paramavyoman*), which is unsurpassed and imperishable.
They say [this is so] because it is impossible for another [moment of consciousness] to arise therein. || 57 ||
Now he concludes the previously stated utility of the *bindu* for conceptual cognition:
"The *bindu* itself [assumes] the name 'conceptual' in conceptual cognitions. (58)
By delineating its own various modes of functioning through their mutual interpenetration, the *bindu* alone attains consciousness (*citi*).
Because it is the material cause of sound, through its connection with the various modes of its own functioning— ranging from the subtle (*sūkṣmā*) up to the manifest speech (*vaikharī*)—
it attains consciousness for itself within conceptual cognitions by delineating the reflective conceptualizations such as "this is a jar," "it is red," or "it is round."

It produces determinate experience (*savikalpakānubhava*). For it is through the penetration of words that determinate knowledge (*savikalpajñāna*), qualified by qualifiers such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, arises. As they say: "First, there is indeed a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition of mere observation (*ālocana*), like the perception of the deaf-mute and others, arising from the pure object itself. Following that, however, [there is a cognition] by which the object is [perceived] through its properties (*dharma*), such as genus and the rest..."

"That [object] too is determined by the intellect and is accepted as being perceptible" (Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa 112, 120). Nor is this mental impression, known as *bhāvanā*, [perceptible], because it lacks the nature of direct perception.
For mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) have memory as their mark; they do not fall within the range of our direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This determinate experience (*savikalpānubhava*) should not be considered an impression consisting of a latent trace (*vāsanā*) of a previous experience, because that [impression] is inferable, whereas this [experience] is of the nature of a perceptual experience. Indeed, it is through the otherwise inexplicability of memory (*smṛti*) that the impression is established.
It is conceptualized. || 59 ||

Is it not the case that determinate experience (*savikalpānubhava*) is merely a specific transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*), since determination is an effect of the intellect? To this he says:
"Nor is it a transformation of the intellect, because [the state] may exist even beyond *māyā*. (60)

It has been stated that even though the intellect (*buddhi*) is the cause of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*), conceptual knowledge is produced only through the cooperation of sound, which is the effect of the *bindu*.

For this very reason, it is established that even in the absence of the intellect in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), the Vidyeśvaras and others possess conceptual experience by means of the power of speech (*vākśakti*). || 60 ||
And then:
"In that way, the Lord of Knowledge, Ananta, having pervaded Māyā with his splendor, then brings about creation, possessing conceptual cognition. (61)
Because he possesses agency while being atomic in nature, he is like a person subject to our command;

since the infinite [Lord] impels [the individual soul] through the remaining impurity of its office by virtue of its atomic status, it is precisely through the connection with conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) that he causes the agitation of *māyā*, and not, as is the case for Śiva’s agitation of the *bindu*, through mere non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka*) alone—this is the intended meaning. || 61 ||

Having thus stated that the Bindu is established as the cause of the Vidyēśvaras and others through the agency of the Infinite One by means of conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) and the medium of sound, [the author] now states the opinion of others regarding this very same point: "Others, who are experts in the doctrine of the differentiation of the transformation of the functional state (*vṛtti-pariṇāma-bheda-vāda*). (62)
Other teachers explain this [verse] with a different interpretation of the qualifying attributes.
Other teachers establish the agency of Ananta in a different manner, through the application of conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) toward this very object as previously qualified.
This [self] is the agent of transformation, but not of the mental state; therefore, it is so. (63)
Since this infinite one is the agent of transformation, the meaning is that he possesses such conceptual knowledge (savikalpaka-jñāna). || 63 ||
He establishes this very point:
"He who knows, 'This [object] thus agitated by me shall certainly accomplish what is desired'—he, being capable, is the agent of transformations. (64)
But for the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), there is no such dependence; thus he says:

"This property [of being preceded by indeterminate cognition] exists in the case of transformative [entities], but it would be otherwise in the case of those possessing mental modifications (*vṛttimat*).
To elaborate on this very point, he states that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) is preceded by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*).
For thus, everyone beholds that which is free from conceptual construction. || 65 ||
The world perceives the object through conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*); otherwise, it would not.

It has already been stated previously that conceptual cognition arises immediately after non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions. For if conceptual cognition were not admitted, non-conceptual cognition would merely manifest the bare object (*vastu-mātra*).

Because [the object] would be common to all things, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions; the meaning is that the restriction such as "this is the cognition of a jar" would be untenable. || 65 ||
And therefore:
even by one who is infinite, [it must be] preceded by a cognition permeated by sound. || 66 ||
If it were held that everything here is cognized and that this [self] performs [the cognition], it would be because of the conceit of awareness, thinking "I cognize with conceptualization. (67)
Since conceptual cognition arises permeated by sound— consisting of internal discourse in the form of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— due to its nature as the realization "I know," therefore,
having first known objects such as *māyā* through conceptual cognition permeated by sound, [one realizes] the infinite, such as agitation (*kṣobha*) and so forth.
It acts [upon itself], because it is not observed that something unknown is being acted upon. || 66-67 ||
However, because Śiva is the agent of the activity (vṛtti), it depends upon the agitation of the *bindu*; thus he says:
"The activity itself is considered to be like a hut for a cloth made from the *bindu*;
therefore, even in non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpakabodha*), the Lord presides over the *bindu*. (68)
And since there must indeed be a dependence on conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) for the infinite transformer (*pariṇāmakartṛ*), he concludes:
"The Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) is not thus; for this Māyā is transformative.
Having thus set forth the opponent's view, he refutes it:
No difference in agent is determined by the modifications of the functions. || 69 ||
"Even for one constructing a hut, the intellect is indeed seen to be conceptual (*savikalpā*).

The word "hi" (indeed) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). This has been stated as a refutation of the opponent's own admission, and not as our own established tenet (*siddhānta*), because there is scriptural authority for the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of even the *bindu* into the form of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth, and because there is no absolute difference between the modification of a state (*vṛtti*) and transformation. || 69 ||
Now he states the synonymous names of the *bindu*:
"The reality of sound (*śabdatattva*), the unvoiced speech (*aghoṣā vāk*), Brahman, Kuṇḍalinī, and the Immovable (*dhruva*). (70)
The teachers have declared that Vidyā is the supreme Śakti, Nāda is Mahāmāyā, Bindu is likewise [the principle], and it is also called Vyoman and Anāhata. (71)
Now he demonstrates the functions of the *bindu*, such as the "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and others, according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*):

"It has four functions by which the three types of individual souls (*aṇu*) are pervaded; by which [functions] the individual souls, as previously described, become possessed of superior, middling, or inferior knowledge and so forth. (70–71)
Regarding the question "Which are they?", he says here:
Vaikharī, that which is known as Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and that designated as Sūkṣmā. (72)
Therefore, the meaning is that the *bindu* is established as the cause of these [energies]. || 72 ||
He describes the nature of *vaikharī*:
therein, *vaikharī* is that which is perceivable by the ear and denotes an object;
and it is—
When the vital air (vāyu) is restrained within its stations, it assumes the grasp of the phonemes (varṇa).
This [articulation] is generally dependent upon the maintenance of life for those who employ it.
Thus they say:
"Sound, originating from space and air, emerging from the body, reaches the mouth."
"That which, being divided across different locations, attains the state of phonemes (varṇa), is sound (śabda).
Regarding the intermediate [speech], he says: "It consists solely of the material cause of the intellect (buddhi), follows a sequence, and conforms to the phonemes. (74)
But that which consists of internal discourse does not reach the ear;
transcending the function of the vital breath (prāṇa), it exists under the name "Madhyamā" (the Intermediate).
And it has been stated that this [power], whose nature is the knowledge of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), is also the cause of the gross word (sthūlaśabda). || 74-75 ||
Through the process of total withdrawal of all phonemes without distinction, Paśyantī is self-luminous, resembling the fluid within a peacock's egg. (76)
And it has been stated that this is in the form of the syllable-bindu (akṣarabindu). || 76 ||
Now, he describes the subtle state, which was previously mentioned as the seed of the intellect regarding the object of expression and is synonymous with *nāda*:
"The light of its own nature alone is the internal, subtle, and non-departing speech.
Its quality of being "non-departing" arises because it exists even in states such as deep sleep, and not because of its eternity. Of this [speech]...
Furthermore, because it is manifold due to its differentiation according to each individual, and because it is insentient and an effect, it has been stated that its cause is indeed the *parabindu*.
He specifies that very [state]:
"In which, when its true nature has been seen, the qualification for action ceases. (77)

In that [state], when its true nature has been perceived through discrimination from the nature of the Puruṣa, the Puruṣa’s entitlement to experience ceases. If this is so, does it not follow that initiation (dīkṣā) is useless, since liberation is accomplished through discriminative knowledge alone? That is not so; because impurity (mala) is a substance, it is removed by the operation of the Lord known as initiation, just as a film over the eye is removed by the operation of an oculist.
Because cessation is established. || 77 ||
And therefore, precisely because of the absence of discriminative knowledge regarding that object, the proponents of Śabdabrahman consider it to be inherent in the person; thus he says:
"In the person consisting of sixteen parts, they call that which is named 'immortal'."
Thus he states that their view is an error:
"The Lord is pure, supreme bliss, steadfast, eternally manifest. (78)
Neither setting nor rising, neither weary nor subject to transformation,
the Sun— whose essence is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman)— moves within all living beings.
Having pierced through that [darkness] with the sword called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), they emerge from it without hesitation;

having pierced, analyzed, and correctly understood this very thing, the selves emerge from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This sun, known as the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), is thus distinct from the [physical] sun.
This is their delusion. || 78-79 ||
Regarding this, he states the established conclusion: "The people who know the Self call that very speech 'the subtle' (sūkṣmā). (80)

The word *eva* (only/just) is displaced in its position [in the verse]. However, the Śaivas who know the true nature of the Self maintain that the function of sound (*śabdavṛtti*) is indeed that which is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*), being an effect of the *bindu*, and not inherent in the *puruṣa*. This is because the *puruṣa* is immutable and insentient; for if it were inherent in the *puruṣa*, the *puruṣa* would consequently incur defects such as mutability and lack of consciousness. || 80 ||
Having thus demonstrated the functions of sound whose nature consists of the effects of the *bindu*, he concludes:
"These functions, restricted to each individual self, are of the nature of bondage.
The meaning is that because these are effects and therefore insentient (*jaḍa*), their inherence in consciousness (*citsamavāya*) is not possible; rather, they are simply bondage itself.
Nevertheless, individuals do not perceive the self as distinct from these [aggregates]. (81)

The meaning is that *pudgalas* are selves (*ātman*) conjoined with impurities (*mala*). The sense is that because the selves are veiled by impurities, there is an illusion of selfhood regarding those very [impurities] due to the absence of knowledge that discriminates them. || 81 ||
To the question, "Whence does this delusion of theirs arise? he replies:

because of the Vedic revelation (śruti) that "the Supreme Self alone is speech" and "speech is the Self," these [passages], which are explanatory statements (arthavāda), [serve] to establish the connection of the Self with the power of speech and so forth.
It is precisely because of their failure to understand the meaning of the Vedas that these persons—meaning those whose selves are joined with impurity—think in this way.
Vaikharī [speech] exists in the cognition born of the ear, while Madhyamā exists in conceptual cognition. (82)
Paśyantī is perceived during the efforts toward the arising of Madhyamā;
Vaikharī is indeed graspable by the ear. Because Madhyamā consists of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is perceived within conceptual thought (*savikalpa*).
Paśyantī is the cause for the production of that [Madhyamā] as well. 82.
But another [verse] says:
"When the repetition [of mental activity], which rests in the mind, has dissolved without remainder... (83)
Then, due to non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the consciousness (*cit*) shines forth as if subtle and pure.

However, it has been stated that the consciousness, which exists in all beings as the seed of the denotable (*abhidheya-bīja*) and serves as the cause even for the *paśyantī* level, appears as if identical to that [subtle form] because of its extreme fusion with it. || 83 ||
And by the logic already stated:
"There is no cognition of atoms that occurs without the accompaniment of words. (84)
In this world, all knowledge arises as permeated by sound.
Furthermore:
This fourfold function [of speech] arises from its dependence on the kalās, beginning with nivṛtti. (85)

It is further divided fivefold; those *kalās* are the functions of the *bindu*. This very function of the *bindu*, whose essence is sound (*śabdātmikā*), serves as an aid to knowledge and the rest for the selves (*ātman*) who are supported by the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, according to their respective degrees of excellence; this is the meaning. As to the question of from where the *nivṛtti* and the others arise, he says:

"Those are the kalās": the meaning is that the kalās are merely states (avasthā) of the bindu itself, being its modal functions (kāravṛtti). Therefore, the point is that the bindu is established as the material cause (upādāna) of the kalās. || 85 ||
He shows those very [calamities] by name:
"Cessation (nivṛtti), establishment (pratiṣṭhā), knowledge (vidyā), and peace (śānti) as the fifth. (86)
These are the kalās that transcend Śānti, by which the fivefold path (adhvapañcaka) is pervaded.
Although these exist as distinct worlds above the world of Sadāśiva, they remain as the nature of Śakti, pervading the entire path; thus he says: "by which the fivefold path is pervaded. (86)
The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), and that consisting of words (padātmaka). || 87 ||

The path of mantra (mantrādhvan) is pervasive among them, while the path of kalā (kalādhvan), resting upon the bindu, pervades the five paths beginning with the principles (tattva). The meaning is that the path of kalā, which has the aforementioned form, rests upon the bindu as its material cause (upādāna). Among these, the path of principles (tattvādhvan) consists of the pure and impure principles beginning with Śiva and ending with earth. As for the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan):

The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is indeed the Mātṛkā, consisting of the worlds beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Kālāgni. The path of words (padādhvan) is that known as Vyomavyāpin. Furthermore, the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) consists precisely of the Saṃhitā-mantras.
But how do these [beings] acquire the designation of "time-periods" (adhvan)? To this he says:
"Having abandoned one by one, and having attained the ageless and immortal state among the Kalās and so forth. (88)
Therefore, the stages beginning with *kalā* constitute the paths traversed by persons.

For just as in the world, along a path, one reaches a village or similar destination by leaving the patch of ground occupied by one foot and reaching the patch of ground occupied by another foot in succession, so too it is with the *kalās* and the *tattvas*.

In initiation (*dīkṣā*), for the sake of experiencing karma in the case of impure objects—whether they be phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), or mantras (*mantra*)—and for the sake of attaining omniscience and other perfections in the case of pure objects, a "joining" (*yojana*) consisting of a specific relationship is performed. Therefore, the series of entities beginning with *kalā* are called "paths" (*adhvan*). || 88 ||
And among those,
the path of parts (kalādhvan) has been previously described according to the divisions beginning with Nivṛtti.
I shall declare its pervasion (vyāpti), together with its support, its signs, and its presiding deities; it has form and cause, and rests upon the Self, the Point (bindu), Power (śakti), and Śiva.

The supports (*ādhāra*) are the heart and so forth; the marks (*aṅka*) are the symbols such as the vajra and so forth; the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) are the governing deities such as Sadyojāta and so forth; the forms (*ākāra*) are the square and so forth; and the causes (*kāraṇa*) are the sovereign lords (*adhipati*) such as Brahmā and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "resting upon the self (*ātman*), the *bindu*, power (*śakti*), and Śiva," it means resting upon those which serve as the substratum (*āśraya*) by being the locus of experience for the selves (*ātman*). Furthermore,

[She is] that [expansion] of which Śiva is the substratum through the function of the limited power (kalā), wherein Bindu serves as the material cause, Śakti as the instrument and the support, and Śiva as the agent. || 89-90 ||
In that regard, he first describes the pervasion of cessation (*nivṛtti*) by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*):
"Within cessation, there is the earthly principle (*pārthiva-tattva*) and one hundred and eight cities;
among those, six [cities] of Kālānala and others are outside the infinite egg (*anantāṇḍa*). (91)
In each of the ten directions, beginning with the east, there are ten Rudras numbering one hundred each, and above them is Vīrabhadra.
And in the world of Bhadrakālī, the phoneme *kṣa* is proclaimed among the letters;

therein, the names of Rudra are indeed the names of the worlds as well. The worlds and so forth have been analyzed and shown by us in the *Paddhati* itself, for fear of excessive length in this work, as they appear frequently in other *paddhatis*.
And because they are well-known, they are not written down here. || 91-92 ||
The Goddess consists of eighty-one words, according to the sequence of the words of re-creation.
Established here by means of twenty-eight words,

the Goddess is the power (śakti) characterized as pervading the void (vyomavyāpin), consisting of eighty-one words. And she, through the sequence of the stages of reabsorption (pratisarga-pada-krama),
beginning from the final *praṇava* according to the order of withdrawal, is established here within the *nivṛtti*-kalā by means of these twenty-eight words.
Moreover:
"But she, that supreme power (kalā), resides there in the hearts of those who have not descended into mantras. (94)
Having pervaded the worlds and so forth, it exists within the five [categories] in five ways;
the meaning is that, having pervaded the five paths (adhvan), it exists within those very [paths]. || 94 ||
Having thus described the pervasion of cessation (nivṛtti), he states its form and other characteristics:
"It is yellow, square, hard, and marked with a thunderbolt. (95)
One should meditate upon her, who has many rising rays of light and is full-bodied, within the lotus of the heart.
He states the cause for the cessation of that [meditation]: "The volitional construction of one whose collection of atoms has dissolved therein ceases" (96).
Because the fruit has not been attained, cessation is thus designated.
Furthermore:
"In this context, Brahman is the cause; Sadyojāta is the presiding deity. (97)

Regarding the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], he also says: "In the *pratiṣṭhā*, however, with the exception of the earth, there are the four [remaining gross elements], the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five organs of action. (98)
The five sense organs, mind, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, and the letters from *ha* to *ṭa* [in reverse order] were present. (99)
Twenty-three [evolutes] have been enumerated, as well as fifty-six cities, located within water, fire, air, ether, intellect, the unmanifest, and ego. (100)
There are eight and eight steps, making twenty-one in number;
the two mantras are Śiras and Vāma, and Viṣṇu is said to be the cause.
She, possessing the luster of a white half-moon and marked by the petals of a blue lotus,
should be meditated upon as shining with abundant light within the lotus of the throat.
Because the volition of that [deity], for whom the multitude of atoms has dissolved, is established for the sake of accomplishing the object,
that digit is therefore called Pratiṣṭhā (Establishment).

For Vāmadeva is considered the presiding deity, whose nature consists of the mantra to be recited. According to the principle that "a mantra is so called because its characteristic is both *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection)—where *manana* is omniscience and *trāṇa* is the grace bestowed upon transmigrating beings—the term 'mantra' applies to Śiva, Śakti, and those favored by them; however, it is used figuratively [in other cases].

This is well known in the case of denotative words (*vācakaśabda*). Therefore, here too, it is precisely the various powers (*śakti*) such as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and so forth, that are spoken of as the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*). For this very reason, the teachers maintain that within those [levels] such as Nivṛtti and the rest—which take the form of worlds—Śiva, possessing the physical forms of Sadyojāta and the others, is the object of meditation for those who desire to attain those respective states. (98–103)
Regarding Vidyā, he says:
"In Vidyā, there are seven persons, along with Rāga conjoined with Niyati. (104)
In that [system], however, the principles of Māyā consist of Vidyā, Kalā, and Kāla;
furthermore, twenty-seven worlds beginning with Māyā are to be known there. (105)
Here, the seven phonemes beginning with *ña* and ending with *gha* are arranged in reverse order;
there are twenty words, and the two mantras Śikhā and Ghora are established [therein]. (106)
Rudra is the cause here, the mantra is Bahurūpa, and the presiding deity is she who possesses many throbbing rays, is triangular, and is marked with a svastika. 107.
One should meditate upon her within the lotus of the palate, possessing a luster like blue collyrium;
for one whose collection of atoms has dissolved therein, volition becomes the range of all objects. 108.
That by which all objects are illuminated is called "knowledge" (vidyā).

Its range is exhaustive, having as its object the entire path (adhvan) situated below its own world; however, it is not "all-encompassing" (sarvaviṣaya), for that is only possible when there is an absence of impurity (mala). || 104–108 ||
In the Śānti [tattva], however, there are three principles and eighteen worlds. || 109 ||
In this [mantra], the phonemes (varṇas) beginning with 'ga' and ending with 'na' are considered to be three;
there were eleven words here, consisting of two mantras: the face and the armor.
Pervading the worlds and other realms, marked by five [triangles] and six bindus,
it possesses the splendor of a thousand rays arising from the hexagon and ending in a small point.
That supreme Śakti should be meditated upon within the lotus at the center of the eyebrows;
for when the multitude of individual souls is absorbed therein, there is an absence of hatred, passion, and other such emotions. (112)
Because of the complete stilling of volitional thought, this is called peace;
therein, the Lord is the cause, and the mantra is that which is named Tatpuruṣa.
The person presiding over that should be known as the adhidevatā;
here there are three principles (tattvas), while the fifth is the supreme power (kalā).
Therein are fifteen cities consisting of the Śiva-tattva;
and those sixteen vowels, preceded by the Visarga, which are designated as *svara*. (115)
The first word, beginning with "Oṃ," consists of the mantras designated as Śiva, Astra, and Īśāna;
it is the supreme digit (kalā) which contains within it the five paths (pañcādhvan) and transcends quiescence (śāntyatītā).
The one to be meditated upon, whose nature is the great space, resides in the lotus of the head;
the Lord, the king of mantras, presides over this cause. (117)
There, the Lord Sadāśiva is proclaimed as the Path of Kalās;
he is all-pervasive, encompassing the worlds and other categories, and is himself pervaded by the Bindu.

This Bindu is pervaded by Śakti and Śiva, and not by anything else. Regarding the phrase "the three": this means those known as Vidyeśvara and Sadāśiva. For this very reason, considering the Śakti-tattva to be included within the Śiva-tattva, he states the pervasion of the Śāntyatītā [kalā]: "But the fifth... He says, "the pervader."

It has been stated that the path of *kalā* (limited agency), which pervades all other paths mentioned, has the *bindu* as its material cause (*upādāna*). Śiva, acting as the agent (*kartṛ*), presides over the *bindu* by means of his inherent power (*samavāyinī śakti*) which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*); however, there is no presiding deity over Śiva himself—this is the meaning.
He says this very thing:
For that God, having encompassed [all things] by His own power which is non-different from Himself, || 119 ||
Having pervaded everything, she perceives and acts;
therefore, it is established that power consists of all knowledge and action. || 119 ||
Now he examines the nature of pervasion (vyāpti):
"The existence of one thing in another, which is always non-deviating," [verse 120].
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the basis for the acquisition of essence, the arising, and the persistence of one thing in another.
For instance, the existence of something else, such as space (*ākāśa*), within another thing, such as a wall (*kuḍya*), at all times without deviation is pervasion.
And that [pervasion] constitutes the basis for the acquisition of essence—that is, the basis for the arising and the basis for the persistence—of the established entity (*āpta*).
Therefore:
"That [power] is twofold when present; it is one through the manifestation of the Supreme Self. (121)
He demonstrates that very point:
"In that regard, consciousness (citi) effects everything by its mere presence, just as the sun is the benefactor of all daytime activities through its proximity. (122)

The *citi* is the inherent power (*samavāyinī śakti*) of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness; by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), it performs the acts of creation and so forth, just as the sun [performs] the blooming of lotuses and the like. For likewise, even in the case of the individual self (*ātman*), agency is observed through mere volition in such matters as the movement of one's own body. 122.
And therefore, he states that the pervasion of the insentient within the Self takes the form of its manifestation precisely through the presiding presence of Consciousness:
"Impelled by Śiva, the Bindu brings about all six paths, beginning with Nāda, within the Self, in due order, through those various transformations. (123)

Just as clay jars and other such objects, when presided over by a potter, [are produced], so too the *bindu* produces all six paths—consisting of *kalā*, *varṇa*, *pada*, *mantra*, *tattva*, and *bhuvana*. Among these, the paths of *tattva* and *bhuvana* are pure in nature; however, the impure paths of *tattva* and *bhuvana* originate from *māyā*.
Furthermore:
That by which a thing is pervaded through its own transformation— (124)
That is declared to be its modification, just as a crown is a modification of gold.
He applies this very principle to the object to be accomplished:
"That sixfold path, beginning with *kalā*, which is pervaded by the *bindu*... (125).
That [universe] is a modification of that [Bindu], because it is pervaded by it, like Nāda and Bindu.

The sixfold path (adhvan), which is distinct from the impure principles (tattvas) and worlds (bhuvanas), leads back to its own cause, Bindu, as an effect—just like Nāda and Bindu; this is the intended meaning. || 125 ||
Now he sets forth the opinion of those who maintain the coalescence of the *bindu*:
"Some declare that the *bindu* coalesces with Śiva; from that [arises the result]. (126)
This supreme Kuṇḍalinī is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), just like the power of vision (dṛk-śakti).
The sense is that, like the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), this other power of action—which consists of the Bindu—also inheres in Śiva; it is not separate from Him, unlike Māyā. || 126 ||
And thus:
"In Śiva, there are two inherent powers, consisting of knowledge and action. (127)
He elaborates on this very point:
"In that regard, the first is consciousness (*saṃvit*), the second is cognition (*vijñāna*), the third is action (*kriyā*), and the fourth is the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*.
The designation 'consciousness' applies to the first, while the designations 'action' and 'the coiled one' (*kuṇḍalinī*) apply to the other."
Of these two, however, it perceives the world through the power of knowledge and acts upon it through its power of action. || 128 ||
The word "Śiva" is to be supplied [as the subject]. || 128 ||
To the question "Why?", he says:
"For action alone bestows fruit upon men; knowledge would not be the giver of fruit.
Since even for potters and others, it is only the power of action—consisting of effort—that results in the production of jars and the like."

The power of action brings about the fruit, whereas the power of knowledge fulfills its purpose solely by making those respective objects its domain. Therefore, Śiva too, cognizing through the power of knowledge, performs everything through the power of action.
And therefore:
He is never separated from those two, nor do they exist without Śiva. (129)
Having thus demonstrated the union of the *bindu* with Śiva according to another school of thought, he shows the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva according to that same view:
"When those two proceed in equilibrium, there arises the principle of Sadāśiva."
Of Īśa and the two superior powers of action (kriyā-śakti), which are distinct from vidyā and jñāna. || 130 ||

When both action (kriyā) and knowledge (jñāna) proceed in equilibrium, there occurs a transformation into the nature of the Sadāśiva-tattva, as in the case of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). However, when the power of action predominates, it consists of the Īśvara-tattva;
and when the power of knowledge predominates, it consists of the Vidyā-tattva.
Furthermore:

Among those principles (tattvas), for the great-souled ones who are isolated in consciousness (vijñānakevalas), there are diverse worlds and beloved wives who delight in their own inherent nature. 131.
Śiva brings about enjoyments that do not fade, as well as the limbs and the organs, through the power (śakti) that is non-different from him and whose nature is action.
For that reason, this agent is considered the creator even of the *nāda* and other [principles] of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).
He summarizes the point already explained:
"Therefore, this is not separate from Power; Power itself is of the nature of action. (133)
"In that [state], it is designated as the *bindu* inherent (*samaveta*) in Śiva.

Therefore, some maintain that this *bindu*, although not entirely separate from the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) inherent in Śiva, is indeed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) inherent therein. Now, in order to refute that view, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). The meaning is that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is being stated.
He says that very thing:
"This [Lord], within himself, [perceives] the multitude of principles and the series of many worlds. (134)
Producing various, manifold bodies, enjoyments, sense organs, and so forth, that which is called *bindu* is logically described as undergoing transformation, just like *pradhāna*. (135)

Since the Bindu is heard in scripture as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth, its state of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) must necessarily be admitted, just like *pradhāna* or clay and other such materials. (134–135)
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
Whatever entity is subject to transformation is necessarily insentient by nature; as, for example, milk. Since this [universe] is insentient, how could its inherence reside in Śiva? (136)
