Furthermore, because it is subject to transformation, its insentience (*jaḍatva*) is established, just like milk and other such substances. Consequently, an inherence (*samavāya*) with consciousness (*cit*) is not tenable for it;
thus he says: "Because of insentience" (verse 136).

He states that if one were to accept an inherence relation (*samavāya*) with that [world], it would follow that even Śiva is insentient: "For that relation of identity (*tādātmya*) would impart insentience to Śiva, whose sole nature is an incomparable, indivisible mass of consciousness. (137)

Of that Śiva, whose single essential nature is a dense body consisting of consciousness and action—a body that is incomparable because it is eternally liberated, undivided because it is the object of all, and a mass of consciousness—this is the meaning: the power whose essence is consciousness is indeed the body of Śiva. And although that [power] is one, it is metaphorically designated as the power of knowledge and the power of action due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the objects of knowledge and their effects.

It partakes of a divine designation. Since it performs the functions of the body through the various states beginning with Īśāna, which assist in the fivefold acts (*pañcakṛtya*), it is figuratively treated as the body; thus, its conjunction with an insentient *bindu* is not tenable, for if such a conjunction were to occur, defects such as insentience would necessarily follow. || 137 ||
If it is argued, "Let him be insentient; what is the fault?", [the reply is:
For that dull-witted person who, out of delusion, conceives of the Lord as insentient, there is neither logic nor scripture, neither a self nor a deity. (138)

If one accepts that Īśvara is insentient, then there is sublation by the inference used to prove Īśvara as the creator of the world, as well as by the scriptures that establish His essential nature as sentient and so forth. Furthermore, since the logic is the same, it would follow that the selves who are of the same genus as Śiva must also be insentient. And of those...
Even as a deity, one does not achieve success by being the agent of worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 138 ||
And therefore:

"He [the opponent] should be avoided by the wise, as he is excluded from all those who affirm existence (sarvāstika). But surely, even in your own position, since Śiva is accepted as an agent, there must be an entry into activity (*kriyāveśa*)."
Is there not the undesirable consequence of [consciousness] being transformed? To this he says:
"Because it is the cause of action, that which is consciousness itself is the power of action. (139)
In this case, there is no actual penetration by action, nor even agency; rather, there is simply the capacity for action.
Consequently, just as the power of a magnet acts upon iron through its mere proximity, the penetration of action occurs in the *bindu* (point) through the mere presence of Śiva’s power.
Therefore, because it is the cause of action, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) itself is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); thus, there is no contradiction. || 139 ||
Here, preceded by a potential objection, he reaffirms what was previously stated in the verse beginning with "Since the pure path arises" (Śloka 22):
"If it is thought that there is no other *bindu* above *māyā*, nor any insentient (*acid*) [reality]," etc.
From where does the pure path arise, or where might it dissolve, and by what means? || 140 ||
This [liberation] is sixfold, through the distinctions of principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and so forth.
How and why, moreover, are the Vijñānakevalas threefold? || 141 ||
They would be liberated even without the *bindu*, which brings about that variety.

[Objection: But surely the very power of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is the cause of all that; therefore, he says: "For consciousness does not effect that [creation] in its entirety through transformation (*pariṇāma*). (142)
That this is due to the nature of consciousness will be explained later in the *Śaktinirṇaya*;
this has already been shown previously, and it has been established by us in detail in our commentary on the *Tattvaprakāśa*. 142.
Here, an objection is raised: "This [Self] may indeed possess various imagined distinctions based on its specific effects. (143)
If it is held that Śiva is indeed one and possesses manifold powers, [we reply:

surely, as has been stated, it is not logical for the conscious Śiva to undergo transformation into the form of the principles (tattvas) and so forth; rather, although Śiva is one, the differentiation of principles such as Sadāśiva and others—based on the diversity of effects arising from his manifold powers—is merely figurative and conceptual, and not [real].

If it is your intention that [the distinction] is indeed ultimate, then that is certainly true; for regarding the subject of the presiding agent (adhiṣṭhātṛ), the distinction between the states of Śiva, the presiding agent, is merely figurative (aupacārika) because it is produced by the distinctions among the objects to be presided over (adhiṣṭheya). However, the distinction of the principles (tattva), worlds (bhuvana), and so forth, within the pure path (śuddhādhvan)—which constitutes the object to be presided over—is truly real, otherwise even figurative usage would be impossible. || 143 ||

Now, if it is maintained that even that [the path] is unreal because it is a transformation of consciousness, then the path consisting of Māyā would likewise be so, since there is no difference in reasoning. (144)
The meaning is that since the admission of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is possible in the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), that [impure path] too would be rendered unreal.
If it is argued, "Let it be unreal; what is the harm?", that is incorrect, because it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says:
"By their respective reasons, by the scriptures, and even by the perceptions of yogins..."
How could a wise person reject the well-known, pure paths? (145)

And here, the mention of the "pure path" (śuddhādhvan) is an elliptical indication that includes the impure principles (tattvas) as well. Therefore, the intention is that those who assert the unreality of the universe—comprising both pure and impure forms—are indeed of poor intellect, for such a position is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 145 ||
For it is thus:
engagement with the Lord, who is distinguished as the most generous giver according to the scriptures, is said to lead both to enjoyment and to liberation. (146)

According to the scriptures, since Śiva is established as the bestower of both enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa), it is observed that individuals engage in activities for the sake of either enjoyment or liberation according to their respective capacities, following the very sequence taught in the scriptures. || 146 ||

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that even the abode of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*) is heard of in the scriptures as being directly created by Śiva and being absolutely pure, he cites the venerable *Mataṅgasūtra* (Vi. 26.63):
"The state of Sadāśiva [is attained] through yoga, or through ritual conduct (*caryā*), or else through initiation (*dīkṣā*)."
Liberation is attained either through the differentiation of the mind or through the fourfold [means]. || 147 ||

By the term "distinction of consciousness" (*cittabheda*), knowledge is intended here. Consequently, since action cannot proceed on the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), and because the enjoyment (*bhoga*) produced by that [action] is impure—consisting as it does of pleasure, pain, and delusion—there exists pure enjoyment known as "inferior liberation" (*aparamokṣa*), which pertains to the worlds of Sadāśiva and the others; and there is also "supreme liberation" (*paramokṣa*), which consists in identity with Śiva.

Liberation is attained through initiation (dīkṣā) assisted by yoga and other means. In that regard, for those who undergo material initiation (bhautika-dīkṣā), liberation is attained after the exhaustion of experiences once the impurity (mala) has reached a state of maturation; for those who possess a specific degree of matured impurity and undergo final initiation (naiṣṭhika-dīkṣā), it occurs immediately after the fall of the body;
and for those who undergo instantaneous liberation initiation (sadyonirvāṇa-dīkṣā), liberation is attained at that very moment. Now, in this [context]...

Is it understood from the Sūtra that all four—initiation (*dīkṣā*), ritual practice (*caryā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and yoga—are equal means for attaining both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)? It is not so, because of a failure to understand the meaning of the passage. For the meaning of the passage there is as follows:

since the station of Sadāśiva serves here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), [liberation results] from yoga, which has as its fruit the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the respective lords of the worlds (*bhuvaneśvara*).

Indeed, attainment in those respective worlds occurs through conduct consisting of the worship of this or that deity, through initiation (dīkṣā) consisting of the conjunction with this or that world, and through knowledge fixed upon the essential nature of the Lord of this or that world; it does not occur through the state of perfect non-conceptuality (samavikalpatā). For even in the case of knowledge and the other means, there is no entitlement without initiation; therefore, initiation alone holds primacy.
Or else, liberation arises from this quartet taken collectively, not from any single one; such is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*), which implies that enjoyment likewise results from them.

Furthermore, in the case of *caryā* (conduct) and *yoga*, practice itself is not possible without knowledge, for neither yoga nor conduct can occur with respect to an object that is unknown. Moreover, knowledge [is required] because the bonds of impurity (*mala*) and so forth are substances, just as [knowledge is required to remove] the cataracts of the eye.

It has been stated that, without the activity of the Lord known as *dīkṣā*, the activity of the eye-physician is not capable of effecting liberation for persons from those [impurities]. Therefore, *dīkṣā* alone is the cause of liberation. And it is said in another section of that very same work:
"Therefore, the mantra-rite presided over by the Lord is primary, for it bestows liberation" (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 7.74).
Also in the Śrīmatṣaṭsāhasrikā: "Initiation alone bestows liberation upon men and brings about the manifestation of consciousness. (147)

And here, it is stated that the state of Sadāśiva is heard of as the locus of enjoyment (*bhoga*): "Thus enjoyment has been fully described; the great state of Sadāśiva [is called so] by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) through the word 'enjoyment' (*bhoga*). This also applies to the term "the state of Sadāśiva."
It has been stated that this is an illustration of the worlds of the pure path (śuddhādhvan).

And because this [universe] is an effect by virtue of having the nature of the world, and because it belongs to the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), it has been stated that the Bindu alone is established as its material cause; with this intention, he says:
"In that [Pure Path], no body, enjoyment, or the like arises with Māyā as its material cause. (148)
Therefore, because of its purity, the pure path (śuddhādhvan) is established for the sake of enjoyment;
therein lies the station of Sadāśiva. || 148 ||
Furthermore, he states [the following] for the sake of proving the pure path (śuddhādhvan):
"Moreover, Māyā is presided over by some agent who is subject to it. (149)
She is the material cause of the kalās and so forth, her very nature being pervaded by the kalās;
for she is indeed like a potter [is to] the clay of jars and other vessels. (150)

By relying on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the effect—ranging from *kalā* down to earth—is pervaded by those *kalās*, which are of the nature of power (*śakti*), acting as its substratum; thus, Māyā, whose essential nature is pervaded by the *kalās*, being impure like clay and so forth, is agitated by an agent impelled by Śiva, but not directly by Śiva himself like the *bindu*. This is stated [in the scripture]: "In the pure path, Śiva [is the agent]."

"The Lord Ananta is declared to be the agent in the case of the dark [deeds]" (Kulārṇavatantra-viveka 3.27). Thus, he shows that even the potter is impelled by Śiva, beginning with "For instance" (tathā hi). 149–150.
The agent is to be impelled by way of the state of being a bound soul (paśu), while Maheśvara is the cause.
The meaning is that because he possesses the state of a bound soul, the potter is the impelled agent, whereas Śiva, due to his stainlessness, is the impelling agent.
For it is said: "This ignorant creature is declared to be powerless even over its own affairs. (151)
"Whether one performs a good or an evil deed, it is impelled by God.
Having thus established this illustration, he applies it to the subject at hand:
"Because He is the one who causes action, the Infinite One (Ananta) is joined with a body and so forth, like a potter. (152)
That path by which Māyā is agitated—whether by means of the body, the senses, or the location and so forth—is purified in the teaching of Śiva. (153)

"By which" means "by that which consists of me. "By space and so forth" means by the substratum consisting of the worlds and the like; because of the inclusion of the word "and so forth," it is joined with the previously mentioned cause of conceptual cognition, namely, speech. The infinite agent is the pure path, as established in the Śiva-scripture. (152–153)

Having thus established Mahāmāyā— known as the Supreme Bindu— which is insentient, serves as the material cause for the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan), and consists of the power of appropriation by refuting other doctrines,
he now presents, according to another doctrine, that even the Impure Path (aśuddhādhvan) has the Bindu as its material cause and that Māyā is its effect:
Other wise scholars call this state of the Bindu "Māyā," because its essential nature is pervaded by Kalās and it is presided over by the Pudgala.

Since even Māyā is pervaded by the *kalās* of the Bindu and is presided over by the Pañcātman from the principle of Śuddhavidyā, they therefore call it too a subtle transformation of the Bindu itself, existing in the form of its effect. || 154 ||
In the same way, their primordial nature (prakṛti) is threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme; therein, the gross form is Mahāmāyā, consisting of the qualities (guṇas). || 155 ||
That *prakṛti* is the producer of the objects of enjoyment, such as the intellect (*buddhi*), for the *puruṣa*.

They say that even *prakṛti* is merely another gross state of that very [bindu]. Thus, for those who maintain that the single *bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna*), that *mahāmāyā* is divided into three types according to the distinction between the gross (*sthūla*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the supreme (*para*).

That gross state of the *bindu*, consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is called *prakṛti* because it produces, through a succession of transformations, the principles such as the intellect (*buddhi*) which are the means of experience for the *puruṣa*, as well as the objects of experience. || 155 ||
Subtle, she is the nature of the non-differentiation of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā. || 156 ||
The deluding Māyā is the mother and the cause of the entire impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*).

However, that which is known as subtle *māyā* is the direct or indirect cause of all things— the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*, which are the causes of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), as well as the worlds (*bhuvana*) and the selves residing within them, including primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
Furthermore:
The supreme Māyā is the source of mantras; she is indeed the eternal Kuṇḍalinī. || 157 ||

The material cause (*upādāna*) of bodies whose selves are the lords of knowledge and ignorance is *māyā*; however, the supreme [cause] is that which has *māyā* as its material cause. This means that *mahāmāyā* is the material cause of *māyā*.
And it is eternal, because it is the ultimate cause. || 157 ||
And therefore:
This illusion (māyā) consists of effects and is subject to transformation. || 158 ||
Then one should establish the agent as being conjoined with a body and sense organs;
and thus, the accomplishment of the pure path remains inevitable. (159)

For those for whom, according to the Māyā doctrine, the impermanent *kalās* such as *avidyā* and the rest are the cause, their path does not become pure through the purification of the *kalās*. || 160 ||

Having thus established the causality of *māyā* according to the view of others, he states the objection regarding the impermanence of *māyā* with the words "of those who... (*yeṣām*). If, due to the impermanence of *māyā*, one does not accept it as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*), then the purification of the Impure Path (*aśuddhādhvan*), which is the effect of *māyā*, could not occur through the purification of the Path of Kalās (*kalādhvan*), which is the effect of the Bindu; for [purification] cannot belong to something other [than its own cause].

Because purity is not possible for anything else [than that which is already pure], therefore, since purity cannot otherwise be accounted for, it must be admitted that even the path of purity (*śuddhādhvan*) is indeed an effect of the *bindu*. (159–160)
He says this very thing:

"For the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, when purified, lead to the purification of the principles (tattvas) and so forth; therefore, the path (adhvan) from the Bindu onwards is particularly the object of [this] action. (161)

The sense is that, since [the universe] is an effect of the Bindu, the purification of all principles (tattvas) and so forth is inevitable through the purification of the Kalās that serve as their material cause. || 161 ||
Now, one might object that through the purification of the pervasive *kalās*, there will follow the purification of the pervaded principles (*tattva*) and so forth; to this he says:
"However, purification in the paths is not considered to result from the purification of the mere pervaders alone."
Of the parts that are without material substratum, and of the two which are eternally pure. || 162 ||
Because the constant state of purity follows from the very purification of Śiva and Śakti, this supreme Mahāmāyā is declared to be the primordial nature (prakṛti) of all the paths. 163.
By those teachers, who are experts in explaining the functions of all the paths,

this position has been diligently refuted because there is no evidence for the impermanence of *māyā* here, because it is impossible for pure *bindu* to have impure matter as its material cause, and because it contradicts scriptural statements regarding its permanence.
Having considered the opinion of the teachers who know the established tenets (*siddhānta*), he says the following to prove the eternity of *māyā*:
"But others say here that *māyā* is imperishable like the sound of a path. (164)
And the substrate (*upādāna*) of the *kalās* and so forth is pervaded by the *bindu*.
This has been stated in the venerable *Svāyambhuva* and other scriptures: "The *māyā*-principle is the seed of the universe, indestructible and of an imperishable nature," and so on.
Also in the venerable *Raurava*: "The Lord of the Sovereign Kings of Knowledge, the King of Mantras, having agitated *māyā*..."
"He produced the *kalā*" (1.6–7), and so forth. || 164 ||

If it is argued that even though *māyā* is not an effect, purification might still occur through the purification of the *kalā* that merely pervades the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), it has already been stated that this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, he says:
"And such a purification of those two is to be known by those who know the scriptures. (165)
It is heard in the scriptures that through the purification of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) itself, the purification of other things dependent upon it occurs;

specifically, through the purification of the pervasive aspect (*kalā*), the purification of the entire path (*adhvan*) that is pervaded is accomplished in initiation (*dīkṣā*) by means of the consumption of karma and so forth. And this is the intended meaning here: when karma exists...

The impure path (aśuddhādhvā), beginning with *kalā*, stands as a bond for individual souls (*ātman*); its purification, in their regard, is intended simply as the cessation of its status as a bond. And that [purification] arises through initiation (*dīkṣā*) for one whose impurity (*mala*) has reached maturity, due to the exhaustion of karma (*karmakṣaya*).
As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇatantra*: "Karma pertaining to many births, even that which is yet to come, is blocked by the souls like a burnt seed."

"For by that [means], this [is achieved] through enjoyment" (Vijñānabhairava 6.19). Also, in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*: "Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is that which causes the exhaustion of merit and demerit. Therefore, since all paths (*adhvan*) are included within each other, initiation—consisting of the enjoyment of experiences and so forth—is possible; thus, through the purification of the pervasive path of *kalā*, there is also the purification of the pervaded, impure paths such as the *tattvas* and *bhuvanas*.
Since purity, characterized by the cessation of the state of being an obstacle toward that [Self] for one whose form is common [to all], is thus established, there is no fault whatsoever.
Having thus stated that there is no fault even though Māyā is eternal, he further qualifies the Bindu itself: "The Great Māyā, who is the source of mantras, abides as the one who embraces. (166)

Mahāmāyā is the womb of all expressive mantras (*vācaka-mantra*), because it is the material cause of sound; since it is impossible for all individual souls (*pudgala*) to arise from the mantras that are expressed (*vācya-mantra*). She is called Śiva’s power of possession (*parigraha-śakti*), by which all bound souls (*paśu*) are pervaded.
As previously stated, they are presided over by means of the channels beginning with nāda. || 166 ||
Furthermore:
This power, whose nature is action, is the Sovereign Goddess who is eternally manifest. (167)
Existing among the bound souls (paśus) alone, it is established as their bondage.

And because this [bondage] is presided over by the Lord’s power of action (kriyā-śakti), and because the souls remain in a state of non-discrimination from that power of action, some have erroneously declared it to be the "Lordly Power of Action" (aiśvarī kriyā-śakti); however, it is not so.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) inheres in consciousness; it has been stated that this is because [the power] is insentient by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*).

For this very reason, it does not operate in liberated souls (*muktāṇu*), as it exists only in bound souls (*paśu*). This [power] also exists solely as a fetter (*pāśa*), and not through inherence in Śiva who is beyond all fetters. || 167 ||
And for this reason—she constantly leads the bound souls (paśus) through various wombs without certainty. 168.

This power of action (kriyā-śakti), when known as non-different [from the Self], binds bound souls (paśus) to impure wombs; however, through discrimination of that [power], there is no attainment of an impure womb—this is the meaning. || 168 ||
Furthermore—by means of the potency (*vīrya*) of self-reflection, it bestows both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
By its own potency, which consists of the knowledge of self-reflection, it bestows enjoyment and liberation. Regarding enjoyment and liberation:
The meaning is that it becomes beneficial through a continuous succession.

Illusion (māyā), however, is conducive to experience, because it is the cause of the cognition of "self" and so forth regarding that which is not-self and so forth; he demonstrates its conduciveness to experience therein:
"By means of being the cause for the arising of the conditions that are the instruments for the attainment of experience. (169)
Through the interpenetration of words, the undiscriminated Great Illusion (mahāmāyā), whose nature remains unexamined, perpetually deludes the bound souls (paśus).

By means of the interpenetration of words— which serves as the cause for the arising of conceptual cognition that functions as the instrument for grasping the means of enjoyment— she always deludes those who have not discerned her true nature.
It deludes. || 169 ||
And at that time—manifesting a distinct separation from the attainment of immortality in every respect. (170)

Then, for that person whose mind is greedy for the pleasure of enjoying sense objects and who is intent upon the enjoyment of sense objects, it causes at that time a complete turning away from the attainment of liberation; such is the meaning. || 170 ||
He also demonstrates its utility for liberation:
"Knowledge is the cause of the supreme nectar as a means; it is the equipment of the bound soul. (171)

The cause of the initiation known as *dīkṣā*, which is the means for attaining supreme liberation, and of the daily rites (*nityakarman*) and so forth to be performed subsequent to it, is precisely the knowledge of discernment (*paricchedajñāna*); for performance is impossible regarding an unknown object, and even in the case of seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), the teacher is primarily characterized by knowledge. || 171 ||
And he states that for that knowledge concerning objects such as Śiva, the *bindu* alone is the means of accomplishment by way of the scripture:
"And that [knowledge] arose from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) through the interpenetration of sound;
the mass of sounds arises from the *bindu*, and the *bindu* arises from the *nāda*. (172)
This *bindu* of the *anāhata* is the cause of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).

"The *bindu* of the *anāhata*" is a designation for *mahāmāyā*, the source of the pure path; and it has been stated that the production of sound from her occurs through the sequence beginning with *nāda* and *bindu*. || 172 ||
In that state, [he exists] as an enjoyer through enjoyments consisting of the body, the senses, and their objects. (173)

Impurity (mala), karma, and māyā are inferred as being pure; for in that regard, since the scripture declares that the Vidyeśvaras and others possess the status of enjoyers (bhoktṛtva), and since enjoyment is invariably connected with the body and other such factors, there must exist impurity, māyā, and karma, which are the causes of the body and so forth— the instruments of impure enjoyment.

Because those [impurities] are impossible there, one infers a pure *adhikāramala* (impurity of entitlement) as the cause of the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) by means of the body and other instruments of pure enjoyment;

a pure auxiliary action consisting of service to the Lord (*īśvarasevā*); and pure *māyā* as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body and so forth. And of these two—the *adhikāramala* and the action consisting of service to the Lord—...

The attainment of the world of Mahāmāyā through two types of *karma*, or the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which is its cause, is what brings about that state; for such [attainment] is possible only for those who have transcended Māyā and whose impurities (*mala*) have been severed. || 173 ||
He states this very point: "Māyā alone is the cause of both purity and impurity, as well as of taints and karma. (174)

He states that the cause of the impurity of Māyā— the contact with which is the cause of both the impurity of the person (pums-mala), which consists of the conceit of "self" and so forth regarding what is non-self, and the karma that is the cause of impure experience, consisting of the performance of acts such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin— is as follows:
Since Māyā is impure when [the subject] is impure, it is considered to be of two kinds.

However, it should be explained that she is not the cause of the *āṇavamala* (the atomic impurity), because that [impurity] is heard of as being an eternal obscuration (*anādyāvāraka*), and because if it were to have a beginning, there would be no possible cause for its obscuration. But surely, karma is also thus beginningless, according to the scripture: "Karma is likewise beginningless" (*Kiṣkindhā-vijaya* 3.7).
If it is argued that since the activity of *māyā* occurs only when karma exists, how can karma be said to be the cause of *māyā*?
It is true that the continuous succession of karma and the body is indeed beginningless by way of its flow, and in the absence of karma, there would be no activity of *māyā* at all;

nevertheless, because the performance of karma is possible only for those possessing a body, and because karma in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) functions through the medium of the intellect (*buddhi*).

There is no contradiction because it has been stated as such due to its abiding within *māyā*. Action (*karman*)—such as agriculture and the like—is also [an effect], because it serves to refine *prakṛti*;

for if it were to refine the *puruṣa*, it would follow that the *puruṣa* is subject to modification (*vikāritva*). Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures that action exists as a quality (*guṇa*) within the intellect (*buddhi*). And for this reason, he says "therefore, *māyā*" to declare that the dyad consisting of *māyā* and *mahāmāyā* is eternally established.
Thus, the sense is that because their effects are dissimilar, it is not possible for *māyā* to have *bindu* as its effect.
When the distinction from the drop is suddenly realized, the conch-shell of impurity is severed. || 175 ||

Since it has been stated that impurity (*mala*), being a substance, cannot be removed by knowledge alone, and since the attainment of the worlds of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) occurs only for those whose impurities have been destroyed by initiation (*dīkṣā*), the destruction of the impurity of qualification (*adhikāra-mala*) occurs through the discriminative knowledge of Mahāmāyā and Puruṣa, which arises by means of the scriptures. || 175 ||

But upon the discrimination between Māyā and the Puruṣa, there is the destruction of the husks of merit and demerit; as it is said: "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37). Consequently, even when action is exhausted, for those whose impurities have been transformed, there remains only the state of the isolated consciousness (*vijñānakevalatva*). However, upon the discrimination between Prakṛti and the Puruṣa, even that [state] does not exist at all.

As it has been stated by the Siddha-gurus: "Since there is no perception of the karma that results in enjoyment beyond the *guṇa*-principles, even the liberation (*kaivalya*) of the Sāṃkhyas is not tenable, because [the cause] has not been destroyed" (Pañcārthabhāṣya, Kārikā 53).
And then:
"Having transcended Māyā, yet remaining connected to Mahāmāyā. (176)
The power (śakti) of the Lord exists for the sake of agitating the bindu;
that is to say, with respect to the practitioner who has received initiation and desires pure enjoyment, the power of Śiva produces the body and other such things from the agitated bindu. || 176 ||
And he is agitated by power—just as the ocean is stirred on its very surface by the agitation of the wind. || 177 ||

In the same way, a single drop of power (*bindu*) pervades the whole through the impulsion of that power. By the analogy of the "milk-insect" (*ghṛtakīṭa*), the drop undergoes transformation in one part, but not in its entirety like milk turning into curd; for if it were so, there would follow the consequence of impermanence and the consequence of an infinite regress. Furthermore:
The meaning is that it pervades the previously mentioned universe by means of its constituent parts (kalās), which consist of its own functional forms. || 177 ||
And stating that this same principle applies elsewhere as well, he says:
"In this way, by means of a single part of his illusory power (māyā), he transforms the whole. (178)
In the same way, the unmanifest (avyakta) is held to pervade its own effects.

Herein lies the distinction between the *bindu* and the two principles of *māyā* and *pradhāna*: these two pervade only their own effects and not that which is above them, because it is impossible for them to proceed further than that. Therefore, because the pure [principle] also pervades the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*).
The initial approach is indeed possible. || 178 ||
Now, he explains that the distinctions such as dissolution (laya) and so forth belong to Śiva through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), due to the different states of the *bindu*:
"In that case, when the *bindu* is unagitated and consists of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), there occurs worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*). (179)

When [the Bindu] is agitated, there is the domain of the Lord; when it has transcended the Bindu, there is dissolution. When that Bindu—which consists of bliss, which is enriched by universal pervasion, and which was previously unagitated—is made the object of Shiva’s power (shakti) for the purpose of agitation, and thus becomes intent upon emission due to the exertion of Shiva’s power, there arises experience characterized by maintenance.

[The state of] *bhava* occurs; however, when [the power] is agitated and its effect has been produced, there is *adhikāra* (active governance) because the power is occupied with its function. When the effect has been withdrawn and [the power] abides in its own nature, there is *laya* (dissolution) because even the power’s function has been withdrawn. || 179 ||
And thus, he states that the distinction between Śiva and Śakti is merely figurative, arising from the difference in their respective functions:
"Indeed, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is one alone, inherent (samavāyinī) in Śiva. (180)
Due to the differentiation of the three kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), she is the presiding deity over dissolution, enjoyment, and authority;
through connection with these, the one God becomes threefold. (181)
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and the Overlord (Adhīśa) possess the functions of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority respectively.

As it has been said: "He is the one with authority, the enjoyer, and the one who effects dissolution, according to their respective designations. By this conclusion of the examination of the Bindu, it should be understood that the examination of Śakti has been introduced. || 180-181 ||
Now he states the definition of power (śakti): Power consists of a vast mass of unimpeded rays. || 182 ||
Ever-arisen, uninterrupted, and consisting of a non-conceptual nature,
she possesses a majesty that is unobscured, free from duality, and without material cause.
Arising as distinct through the illusory transformations (vivarta) resulting from connection with various limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
she is most proficient in pervading the points (bindu) of the manifold (prapañca), both quiescent and emergent.
Independent of others, not to be manifested by another self, facing every direction, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and free from all bonds. || 185 ||

The culmination, the ultimate limit, the supreme, the subtle, and the state of intense longing for the mere reality (*vastumātra*); here, it is the abundance of knowledge and action. Because even conventional differentiation is absent in this state of dissolution (*layāvasthā*), it is said to be of a non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpasvarūpiṇī*). [Regarding the word] "vividha" (various):

The meaning is that, due to its connection with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of diverse effects, it appears as if possessed of an unreal differentiation arising from its own nature; that is, during the state of engagement with various functions, it is perceived as if divided. Furthermore, she is capable of pervading the *bindu* which is the source of the aforementioned phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*); because she is free from impurity (*mala*), she is independent of anything else and thus cannot be illuminated by another. Therefore...

Thus, by virtue of the distinctness of her own power, she is endowed with qualities such as the liberation from all bonds. She is the *kāṣṭhā*, the unsurpassed; the *niṣṭhā*, the ultimate limit of excellence;
the *parā*, the subtle, the exceedingly subtle; and she is to be understood as the *atilālasā*, whose nature is to bestow grace upon all. (182–185)
And she says that this is indeed the consciousness of Śiva, consisting of knowledge and action:
"The consciousness of the Supreme Lord is considered to possess unfading majesty. (186)

In the very presence of Śiva, who is devoid of any previously acquired particularity, by means of that [power] which is eternal in nature, there arises a specific relationship through this [manifestation]. (187)
The Bindu, repeatedly filling the atomic space of consciousness with its resonant sounds, transforms it as if veiling it with diverse modes of activity.
Just as a river, due to its proximity to the moon, transforms through its surging waves while filling the sky with sound when near the sun; || 189 ||

He states that the *bindu* is the producer of effects through its connection with Śakti, which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*), in the presence of Śiva, who is the agent (*kartṛ*): "of Śiva," etc. It has already been stated previously that the *bindu* fills the consciousness of individual selves (*ātman*) with *nāda*s that are distinct for each person. (186–189)

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that agency is untenable for one who is devoid of sense organs and the like? This is not so; for we observe that even in the movement of one's own body and so forth, the Self acts by means of its mere power (*śakti*) as an instrument. Furthermore, since there is no transformation [of this power] through inherence in Śiva, the distinction between will, knowledge, action, and so forth, arising from the diversity of effects, is merely figurative. Thus he says:
This very power, which rests upon Śiva, is unfailing and full of strength;
though it is one, it is perceived as manifold through the differentiation of its effects.

Just as the single power of the Sun [performs its functions] through actions such as giving and taking, he elaborates upon this very point: "The immutable Consciousness (cit), though performing even that which is not an act of will, is itself Will (icchā) when it effects the work of Will. (191)

In this way, even though knowledge is essentially ignorance and action is likewise non-action, there is a distinction between them as knowledge and action due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the object of knowledge and the effect of action; this is the meaning. || 191 ||
What need is there for more? Whatever function is determined for her by both scripture and the world— || 192 ||

Thus, this embodied Śakti, possessing inconceivable majesty, performs [these functions]. By this, her status as the substrate of all is stated. As they say: "There is no aspect of existence whatsoever residing in either of the two continuums (the individual or the universal) in which the pervasive aspect of Śiva is not found as its presiding controller."
He confirms that very capacity for accomplishing all aims without undergoing change by means of an illustration: "A single wish-granting tree bestows even many objects of desire. (193)
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem possesses various and inconceivable powers of greatness,
so too does she whose singular nature is devoid of any superimposed specific mental impressions (saṃskāra).
The inconceivable power of the All-pervading Lord is capable of performing every purposeful action; yet, because it is consciousness, it undergoes no modification. Thus he says:
"It is not born, nor does it die; it neither wanes nor waxes. (195)
Consciousness (citi) is power because it is luminous and non-inert;
he establishes this very point by means of a negative argument:
"But that which, on the other hand..."
It arises or perishes, and it accumulates or diminishes. || 196 ||
Just as the body and so forth are seen to be either non-luminous in nature or insentient, so too is this [Self] not like them; therefore, it is not subject to modification.
The meaning is that since she is neither of the nature of non-luminosity nor insentient (jaḍa), she is therefore not subject to modification. || 196-197 ||

Thus, by the analogy of milk and curd, any transformation in its entirety has been refuted; now, by means of those very same reasons already stated, he declares that even partial transformation does not exist:
"By those two very teachings, transformation is refuted."
For the transformation of the power of consciousness into non-consciousness is indeed observed. || 198 ||
He elaborates on this very point:
"Resorting to that which is unchanging through transformation, eternal, and auspicious, consciousness does not undergo transformation because of its identity [with it] through inherence. (199)

The power of consciousness (cicchakti), which is eternal, conscious, and auspicious, and which rests upon [Śiva] through inherence—that is, by way of a relationship characterized as identity—cannot be subject to transformation. As it is heard in scripture:
"The power of consciousness is not insentient" (Mṛgendrāgama-vṛtti 3.4). || 199 ||
And therefore:
"This [consciousness] is eternal because it is the cause of all effects, just like Īśvara;
furthermore, it is said to be like a *bindu* because it is devoid of causes in its state of existence. (200)
The intended meaning is that if this [non-existence] were also impermanent, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress. || 200 ||
For, depending upon her, other virtuous beings are eternally existent; for when she is established, the world is established, and when she is not established, nothing exists at all. (201)
Whose existence is established, or by whom is it demonstrated?

For the very existence of that power—the agent and presiding controller of the *bindu* and other [principles] which serve as its material cause—is what establishes the world in its form of effects, consisting of both the pure and the impure; otherwise, it would not exist. By what other means could its existence be proven?

Is it established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? The intention is that it is established precisely by the impossibility of the production of the effect otherwise (*kāryotpattyanyathānupapatti*). || 201 ||

Having thus established the power (śakti), he presents the view of those who maintain the non-duality of consciousness and the unconscious: "Some wise men proclaim this very [power] as non-dual. (202)

"Consciousness (*citi*), which possesses the splendor of the manifestation of the transformations (*vivarta*) of both existent and non-existent forms"—this is an objection raised by the learned (*vipaścit*). For they think as follows: "Power alone, whose nature is consciousness, is the reality;
and it, through the mode of transformation (*vivarta*), manifests objects such as pure and impure worlds, which are unreal. And therefore—
The appearance of duality is indeed an error, just like the cognition of two moons and so forth. || 202 ||
He states this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as a rope causes the illusion of a snake, a hole, or a garland. (203)
It does not produce those objects that are non-existent; rather, it makes them manifest.
In this same way, this mere cognition appears as one or many due to delusion.
And therefore:
This very delusion is without objective support and contradicts all logic;
because its root has been severed through investigation, it is not the cause of either bondage or liberation. (205)
Therefore, upon investigation, there is no bound soul, nor another who binds;
there exists only the eternally liberated, non-dual, and infinite consciousness alone. (206)
But how is it that this appearance of difference is also perceived?
However, conventional practice, which consists of difference, should be understood as being like a yakṣa in a banyan tree. (207)
How, then, is the appearance of difference invalid? To this he says:
"For the difference between entities is not perceived by sensory cognition. Why is that? To this he says: "Sensory cognition."
The cognition of an object that is free from conceptual construction is indeed like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth. // 208 //

The meaning is that since only non-conceptual cognition produced by the power of the object is perception, and it is precisely that which is accepted as valid, difference—being of the nature of conceptualization—is not established by perception. || 208 ||
Furthermore, that [perception] is the establisher of positive entities and does not negate anything.
As it has been said: "The wise declare that perception is an establisher, not a negator" (*Brahmasiddhi* 2.1). And therefore:

The point is that since the apprehension of difference is preceded by the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), its apprehension by perception, whose object is a positive entity (*bhāva*), is not tenable.
But determinate [perception] is that cognition of qualifiers which is preceded by the mental impression of words. || 209 ||

Furthermore, that cognition which arises from the capacity of the object itself is not produced by the senses in dependence on place, time, and so forth; it is considered to be like memory and conceptual construction. (210)

Furthermore, that conceptual cognition which is produced by the senses through the interpenetration of words and in dependence upon place, time, and so forth—this, because it depends on place, time, and so forth, is not produced by the causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*) of the object, like memory or mental imagery;

therefore, it is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As they say: "Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)" (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.4).
For this very reason:
"In that case, inference and scripture are not valid means of knowledge because of their absence;
since entities lack the status of being objects of perception, inference and scripture are also not valid means of knowledge regarding their difference."
They ought to come into being.
For it is thus:
even with respect to an object that is directly perceived, there are indeed objects of conceptual construction as well. (211)
Since even those two [means of knowledge] can only function as valid authorities by producing conceptual constructions regarding an object already established by perception—

given that the apprehension of relations and so forth is preceded by perception and is itself conceptual in nature— it has been stated that the apprehension of difference by means of perception is impossible; therefore, this [notion of difference] is indeed unreal, like the cognition of dreams and the like.
The appearance of difference. || 211 ||
Since this person of deluded intellect is bound by the nooses of doubt arising from himself,
he is liberated from those very same nooses; thus, bondage and liberation do not exist in reality.
Having thus presented that opinion, he introduces the established conclusion (siddhānta):
"Thus, those possessed by the grasp of non-duality, while prattling on, are enlightened by compassionate gurus who bestow the traditional scriptures of the established conclusion. (213)

How is it awakened? To this he says: "If this non-dual consciousness were established by means of empirical instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then by those very means it would certainly become dual. (214)

If you seek to establish the oneness of consciousness for the world by means of the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) established through worldly transaction, then by those very means—which are themselves real—non-duality (*advaita*) is lost. Alternatively, if those [means] are also held to be unreal, then non-duality remains unestablished due to the absence of any means of knowledge; such is the sense [of the argument]. || 214 ||

In order to elaborate upon this very point, he states the nature of inference: "The subject, the example, and the reason, when well-known [independently], are sufficient for the establishment of a property that is not yet established, provided they are reinforced by pervasion (vyāpti). (215)

For, having grasped the pervasion—the relationship of inseparable concomitance—between smoke and fire in the kitchen, which serves as the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), one then infers the property consisting of the possession of fire by means of the reason (hetu) of the possession of smoke in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin), such as a mountain and so forth.
Therefore, the subject and other factors must be accepted as established as distinct and separate entities. || 215 ||
For instance:
A property that is already established is not proven by means of those [reasons] which are themselves unestablished;
nor can establishment and non-establishment coexist in a single place. (216)
For that which is already established does not require another means of proof, nor do unestablished reasons and so forth establish what is established.
And for this reason: inference would be the means of valid cognition for the distinction between the similar class (sapakṣa) and the subject class (pakṣa);
for if there were identity between the two, there could be no similarity of the reason (hetu-sādharmya).

Since, when the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) are identical, there can be no similarity of the reason (*hetu-sādharmya*)— namely, the possession of smoke as the reason established in the example— with the possession of smoke in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), therefore, when those two are identical, the thesis is not established through inference. || 217 ||
But since the apprehension of pervasion is not possible in the absence of an example, he says: "Because of its absence" (verse 217).

He states that if inference is accepted for the purpose of establishing the non-duality of reality in this way— asking "of what, by what, and how is there pervasion?"— then difference will necessarily arise:
"Thus, for the sake of establishing non-duality."
The application, when employed, reveals the distinction for the sake of establishing its own constituent parts.
The meaning is: for the sake of establishing one's own position, such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth. || 218 ||
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "consciousness is one," he says that while this negates a difference in the objects of consciousness, it does not negate a difference in the objects of speech:
"In his view, even the negation would apply to consciousness;
therefore, the state of duality would certainly be established elsewhere, even if [consciousness] were established. (219)
Their thesis is undermined, as it is manifested merely by their own expectations;
even if the authority of scripture is accepted, non-duality is lost. Thus he says:
"Even scripture, for them, [is established] through the particular objects remembered by this or that [tradition]. (220)
How could the collection of objects, as qualified by their mutual relations, be expressed, if this non-dual consciousness were intended to be denoted by itself? (221)

If non-dual consciousness were intended to be expressed by its own means of verbal communication (āgama), how could it produce a qualified cognition— consisting of the synthesis of a collection of word-meanings whose specific objects are recalled by words such as "this cow," "white," "goes," or "to the village," which denote genus, quality, action, and substance? This is what has been stated:

It occurs as follows: if scripture (*āgama*), being true, is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then by virtue of that, its constituent parts and its objects—such as substances (*dravya*) and so forth—must also be real; therefore, this very [position] contradicts non-duality (*advaita*).
And for this reason:
How can scripture or inference establish non-duality, when they are themselves countered by their own constituent parts, which are capable of destroying that very non-duality? (222)

Now, in order to demonstrate that non-dualistic scriptural statements such as "Indeed, the power of consciousness is one alone" cannot have their primary meaning because they contradict other means of valid knowledge,
he says: "Furthermore, words, due to contradiction, abandon their primary meaning..."
For indeed, [words] are seen in both common usage and the Veda to be used in a secondary sense. || 223 ||
Statements such as "this Brāhmaṇa is a cow" or "the sacrificial post is the sun" [are not valid].

However, in the case of inference, once the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—characterized by the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—is grasped, its capacity to establish an object as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed unavoidable; thus he says:
It is not the case that a reason would fail to establish the probandum when the pervasion is unimpaired.

And for this reason, since they are sublated by the inferences that establish difference, the scriptural texts concerning the oneness of consciousness are intended as praises based on similarities such as its eternity and omnipresence; thus he says:
"Therefore, by the force of these reasons, the scriptures [which speak of] duality among selves..."
Even setting aside the primary meaning, cognitions offer praise.
Furthermore:
Even non-conceptual perception grasps the distinction of an object from others in the form of its exclusion [from them], provided that it does not fail to arise. (226)
Being born, [the cognition] is preceded by the recollection of specific details such as names;
it is conceptual, free from doubt, and devoid of error. (227)

In this context, even a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) that arises preceded by the recollection of specific details such as names and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the form of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is non-doubtful and uncontradicted. As they say: "Therefore..."
Furthermore, that cognition by which the ultimate object is determined through its properties such as genus and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.

(Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣa 120). Therefore, that very non-conceptual cognition by which such perceptual knowledge arises also necessarily apprehends the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or difference of the object from other things, because the effect inherits the qualities of its cause and because of the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). || 226–227 ||
However, he states that if the apprehension of difference were not admitted for that [perception], then subsequently no conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) would arise:
"Otherwise, it is not possible."
For one who has not grasped the distinction between objects, it is like the specific qualities of their names and so forth.

Now, it was argued that since difference (*bheda*) is preceded by the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), its apprehension by perception—which has positive entities as its object—is not possible; however, that is incorrect. For this mutual non-existence exists only when difference is already established. Otherwise, one seeking milk would run after fire; thus, everything would be incoherent. (228)
The efficacy of inference also depends upon the apprehension of difference;

for since the apprehension of difference is necessarily required for the sake of the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti) within the relationship of the grasping of pervasion, its existence [is established].
The meaning is that such is the operation of inference.

However, since the mere apprehension of the general entity (*vastusāmānya*) is already established beforehand, inference does not proceed for the purpose of proving a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) by means of a qualification of the subject (*dharmin*). Thus he says:
"Because [the probandum] is already established in the case of the general. (229)
Otherwise, he states the proof of difference:
"Furthermore, if one accepts the otherness between non-duality and difference, then difference would be established; yet in this way, only non-otherness is proven. (230)
If non-duality is accepted as being distinct from duality, then two entities consisting of both duality and non-duality cannot be established.

Alternatively, if it is maintained that even these two entities—consisting of duality and non-duality—which are themselves the distinction between non-duality and duality, possess oneness, then you are merely calling "duality" by the name "non-duality"; thus, there is no dispute between us regarding the name. For we also maintain this very same [view].
Difference alone is what is being established. || 230 ||

But has it not been stated that, just as there is the delusion of a snake and so forth in a single rope, there is the appearance of a plurality of real objects within a single consciousness that is itself real? To this he says:
"The probandum is not established by a mere example; therefore..."
The example of the rope is solely for the purpose of dispelling the confusion of the disciple. || 231 ||

The meaning is that a mere example, being devoid of the reason (*hetu*) and other factors, lacks the power to establish a point; thus, even if the example itself were real, it would contradict non-duality (*advaita*). If, on the other hand, the example were unreal, it would follow that consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*), would also be unreal. Therefore, the illustration of the rope is entirely useless. || 231 ||
Furthermore:
Nor is it identical with consciousness, because no specific qualities of the rope are perceived; nor does it transform into those entities that would cause the cessation of mere cognition. (232)

For indeed, errors such as [the perception of] a snake in a rope and so forth cease upon the arising of correct knowledge; therefore, because they are sublated, the appearance of the snake and so forth is produced by defects such as cataracts and is strictly unreal. However, the manifestation of objects such as jars and cloths persists even at other times and in other places.

Because it appears together with those various entities such as jars and cloths—which, due to the non-perception of any distinction [from it], appear as nothing other than mere cognition, and which are real precisely because they are uncontradicted—the self-consciousness (ātmasaṃvit), though undergoing a phenomenal transformation (vivarta) along with them as limiting adjuncts (upādhi), appears itself as if divided; thus, it does not share the same nature as a rope [which is merely illusory]. This is what is meant:

The distinction between external objects such as jars and cloths is indeed real; however, the distinction in the determinations (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect—which takes on the respective forms of those various objects when they are present—is caused by limiting conditions (*upādhi*) affecting the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvit*). This will be elaborated upon later. Therefore, regarding that form belonging to the intellect, which arises in proximity to each respective object and consists of a determination—

Even though cognitions (*jñāna*) are manifold, there is no change into another form for the apprehending consciousness (*grāhaka-saṃvit*), which appears at all times in a single form as the respective determiner (*adhyavasātṛ*); rather, it possesses precisely eternity, because it is immutable due to its nature as consciousness (*cetanatva*).
Therefore, the self-consciousness is not merely one; for if it were one—
"We have stated elsewhere that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of faults such as the equality of enjoyments and the lack of liberation. (232)

He states that for bound souls (paśu), the delusion regarding the manifold nature of this self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvit*)— arising from a failure to distinguish it from the determinations of the intellect (*bauddhādhyavasāya*)— is caused solely by impurity (*mala*):
"But that consciousness, when unrecognized, evolves through various states of being."
Just as the moon appears to a beast whose power of vision is obstructed by impurity, so it is for the person [whose vision is obscured]. || 233 ||

Just as to one whose vision is obstructed by cataracts even a single moon appears as if it were many, so too, consciousness—which is essentially of the nature of sentience—though unitary, manifests as if having manifold forms due to the power of knowledge being obstructed by impurity. || 233 ||
And just as the cognition of multiplicity regarding the moon— whose unity is established by other means of valid cognition— is caused by a visual disorder (*timira*),

so too the delusion of manifold forms in cognition— which has the nature of the grasper and whose unity is established by scripture and other authorities— indicates its own cause, namely, impurity (*mala*). Thus he says:
Just as one afflicted by cataracts, even while reasoning with a thousand arguments, repeatedly perceives that single moon as many; || 234 ||
Or just as one whose sense of taste is corrupted by bile, even when imagining something sweet, perceives it as bitter due to the defect of the sensory organ. (235)
Just as when water mixed with collyrium is being boiled, even for the wise there arise the distinct cognitions of "blue" and "hot" due to a lack of discrimination [between the properties]. (236)
Thus, having been correctly examined through scriptures accompanied by logical reasoning, it is seen to undergo transformations, appearing as "born," "perished," or "various. (237)

One should bring about the cessation of [obscured] knowledge by means of a cause, just as in the case of cataracts and the like. Furthermore, that impurity, being a substance, does not cease through mere knowledge, but rather—like a cataract in the eye through the intervention of a physician—it ceases only through the intervention of the Lord known as *dīkṣā*. Thus he says:
That [is attained] through devotion to Śiva and by means of that which is proclaimed in the Śiva scriptures. || 238 ||

It can be turned back by action alone, and not otherwise even by millions of knowledges, just as cataracts and the like are cured only by the medical treatment prescribed in the treatises on health. (239)

That impurity is removed solely by the rite called initiation (*dīkṣā*), as taught in the scriptures of Śiva, which is performed as an auxiliary to the meditation on Śiva. As it is said in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*: "Initiation alone liberates and leads one upward to the abode of Śiva.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:

Impurity (mala) is not removable by knowledge, because it conceals the nature of the Self, like cataracts (timira). Impurity is ultimate (paramārtha), because it performs the causal function of causing defilement, just as the impurity consisting of cataracts produces delusion. || 238-239 ||

Having thus stated that the cognizer’s consciousness would otherwise entail permanence, and having explained the impurity as well as its cause of cessation, he declares that the diversity of the objective world (*grāhya-prapañca*) is real:
"Even when there is difference in place, time, and person, [the object] does not appear otherwise."
And how could an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of consciousness be uncontradicted by the means of valid cognition? (240)

Furthermore, it has been stated that the manifold world (*prapañca*) is illusory (*māyeya*) and established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the multiformity of consciousness itself exists only through error; thus he says:
"Therefore, [the world] evolves as a transformation (*vivarta*) from consciousness alone, due to the bondage of the atoms. (241)

He elaborates on this very point: "Indeed, the illusory transformation (vivarta) of the power of consciousness is a false modification, by which [the world], though not having that nature, is experienced as if it possessed that nature. (242)
And he says that this illusory manifestation (vivarta) occurs for the selves due to the non-discrimination of the intellect:

"That [manifestation], which pertains to both the conscious and the unconscious and is mutually connected between the two, arises from non-discrimination because it is accomplished through mutual superimposition. (243)
He explains this very point:

"In that regard, consciousness (cit), due to the non-discrimination between its own nature and the intellect-principle (buddhi-tattva) with which it is connected, [appears] as having superimposed upon itself the modifications of that [intellect], even though it is changeless. (244)
Following birth and so forth, [the intellect] shows the individual self (aṇu) as "born," "perished," "various," "possessing happiness," and "possessing suffering. (245)

In the same way, by superimposing consciousness upon the insentient self and attributing the quality of sentience to it through non-discrimination, one thinks, "I am the child," or "I am thin. Thus [ends verse 246].
This [ego-sense] is common to all atoms, caused by impurity; it is the root of the continuum dominated by delusion regarding the entities of consciousness and the insentient. 247.

This non-discrimination (*aviveka*) of persons, which consists in the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self within that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self, is not without cause, for if it were, it would follow that even one who is liberated [would still possess it]. Therefore, it must have some beginningless cause.
Since non-discrimination is established as beginningless, that which is its cause is *mala* (impurity); such is the sense. (244–247)
He states the reason for this very point:
"For the various manifestations (*vivarta*) of specific consciousnesses with specific insentient objects cannot be joined together without a firm bond. (248)

And this is the underlying intention here: because the selves are veiled by impurity (mala), the manifestation of knowledge and other qualities occurs only through the medium of the limited powers (kalā) and so forth;
and since Māyā is delusive, that manifestation takes the form of the conceit of selfhood (ātmābhimāna) with respect to what is not the self and so on. || 248 ||
He elaborates on the very fact that these two are the cause of bondage: "For instance, the notion of 'I' occurs with respect to the body, not with respect to a clod of earth;
and even that [notion of 'I'] belongs only to someone [specific], namely the subtle self (aṇu), and not to everyone. Therefore, bondage is held to belong to those two. (249)

The remainder [of the argument] is that, between these two—the conscious and the insentient—it is precisely the mutual superimposition of their respective attributes that serves as the regulator of bondage. || 249 ||
Furthermore:
Those sense organs which belonged to a man for the sake of knowledge and action do not likewise serve as instruments for those two functions for another person. (250)
Only a specific cognition is prevented from undergoing transformation;
not every cognition of everyone is so barred. Therefore, bondage is held to belong to those two [the specific cognition and its object]. || 251 ||
Whatever pleasure or pain, in whatever manner, is mounted upon the intellect and experienced by the person, by that [experience] their bondage is determined. (252)

This is the meaning: since, in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the scriptures report that the knowledge and other qualities of all objects—which constitute the very nature of the selves—are not perceived, there must necessarily be an impurity (*mala*) that veils them.

Furthermore, because those selves are observed to possess only limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), there must be a cause for that [limited state] produced through the medium of *kalā* and the other categories; this cause is delusion (*moha*), which acts as the basis for erroneous cognition.

It must be admitted that there exists a bond called *māyā*. Since experience—consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth—as well as the instruments of experience—the body and the senses—are restricted to each individual soul and are diverse, one must necessarily accept karma as the cause of this diversity. (Verses 250–252)

To this, he raises an objection according to the perspective of the Sāṃkhya: "If non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is the regulator here, then let that alone be the regulator; what is the use of postulating for the *puruṣa* a bond called 'impurity' (*mala*) that is not well-known?"—namely, "If non-discrimination is the regulator..."
He refutes [this]:
"By what is that [distinction] between those two produced?
By whom was the mutual non-discrimination between those two—the intellect (*buddhi*) and consciousness (*saṃvit*)—produced? If it were causeless, it would exist even for one who is liberated."

Therefore, one must admit the existence of a beginningless obscuring impurity (*mala*) as its cause, in the absence of which there is no further lack of discrimination for the liberated soul; and it is for this very reason that the existence of the Lord (*īśvara*), the liberator from bondage, has been established. Thus he says:
"Therefore, bondage exists, and bondage is considered to be entirely distinct from the Lord. (253)
And therefore—Bondage consists in the state of being deluded regarding the Self; liberation is the release from that bondage.
When bondage has dissolved in every respect and the atomic impurity (āṇava-mala) has been liberated, [liberation is attained]. || 254 ||
The power that illuminates all objects is the unfolding of Śiva alone;
and it has been stated that both bondage and liberation arise solely through the grace of Śiva. || 254 ||
This most exalted power is liberated from all obscurations. || 255 ||
Having encompassed a very small portion of the objective field, she indeed manifests it.
To the question "How does she manifest it?", he says:
"Of the power whose nature is supreme consciousness, when there is no bondage... (256).
The supreme alone would shine incessantly for liberated souls;

because they are free from impurity, in the consciousness of the liberated self—which illuminates both itself and others—it is the supreme alone, the mere existence of the supreme reality, that shines forth.
The meaning is that it does not shine as a specific object of enjoyment, as it does for bound souls.
For if that were the case, it would follow that even one who is liberated would be an experiencer, due to the perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 256 ||
Therefore, those who are liberated are omniscient, but they do not perceive mere consciousness alone. || 257 ||
But they do not rest in mere self-awareness; rather, like Śiva, they are indeed omniscient. || 257 ||
And therefore:
if an external object exists, that ignorance regarding the thing would be caused by darkness (*tamas*).
Furthermore, even though an external object exists, this mere ignorance of the object is seen by bound souls.
That [bondage] is produced solely by that [ignorance]. Therefore, he says: "For those who are shrouded by darkness do not become liberated. (258)
And he states that the dependence of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) upon the penetration by sound is the cause of bondage:

"Conceptualization arises for individual souls (*aṇu*) obstructed by impurity (*mala*), through the penetration of sound caused by the agitation of the *bindu*, during the perception of objects. (259)
From the unshakeable state of the stainless *bindu*, there arises the non-conceptual realization of reality, born from the bondage and liberation of that *bindu*, like that of a newborn infant.

For the liberated ones, however, because they have transcended the bonds of both māyā and bindu, there can arise no conceptual (savikalpaka) intellectual cognition (bauddhajñāna) assisted by the penetration of sound; rather, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) itself, independent of anything else, takes the object to be grasped as its domain.
And the comparison "like a newborn infant of that very day" should be understood as referring merely to the state of being devoid of conceptual constructions such as sound and so forth. || 259-260 ||

Because even for an ordinary person, objects are not perceived according to their true nature due to being veiled by impurity (*mala*), whereas for the liberated, because they are free from impurity, that power perceives every object exactly as it exists; thus he says:
"Whatever entity exists—whether past or future—at whatever time, [that very thing is perceived at that time]."
The imperishable consciousness, which is self-cognizing, grasps the state of things as they truly are.

Thus it is said in the *Mokṣakārikā*: "With the eye of consciousness empowered by the rays of the power of Śiva’s sun, the self, its veil removed, beholds Śiva together with [His] powers and other attributes" (verse 111). || 261 ||
And he says that even though omniscience and omnipotence are possible for them, they do not engage in creation:
"They are not the creators of the universe, for Śiva alone is its creator.
To the question "Why?", he says:
For there is nowhere to be found any indicator of a plurality of agents. || 262 ||
For even in the case of things like chariots, which have many makers, it is never observed that they come into being without following the will of a single architect.

As it has been said: "Where there are many leaders, all of whom consider themselves wise, and all desire greatness, that undertaking clearly comes to ruin. By this, the position of a succession of gods (pravāheśvara) is also refuted, because of [the instability of] sovereignty.

Because they possess the nature of attaining the manifestation of their own essential form, they are not subject to destruction; therefore, since the effect is brought about by Śiva alone—who is eternally liberated and free from passion, hatred, and the like—they do not engage [in worldly activity]. || 262 ||
He demonstrates this very point: "The power known as Śakti, which is eternally free, ever-arisen, and of inconceivable influence, perpetually rests upon Śiva, the supreme cause. (263)
Having pervaded that [Māyā], the Blessed One, by means of it, creates, maintains, and destroys; He likewise conceals Himself and bestows grace upon His own [souls]. (264)

By this conclusion of the investigation into power (*śakti*), it should be understood that the introduction to the investigation of Śiva, who is its substratum, has also been accomplished. For instance, since the universe possesses a structured arrangement and so forth, it is an effect; and since individual souls are veiled by impurity (*mala*), Śiva is established as its agent, both as the creator of the world and as the one who effects their liberation. As it has been said: "The universe under dispute..."
"Everything is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is an effect, just as our mutual agreement establishes that effects such as jars and the like [have such a creator].
Now, he describes its differentiation through metaphorical designation based on the distinction of its functions:
"In those functions, this agent is said to be threefold, or fivefold."
To the question "How so?", he says:
"The Guru is one who possesses power, has exerted effort, and has set forth," according to the teachers. (265)
He elaborates on this very point:
"In that regard, the first [power] is capable and designated as the partless Śiva;
within him, the sovereign power called Action remains as if in a bud. (266)

To demonstrate that the distinction between knowledge and action is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to the oneness of power (*śakti*), power is referred to by the word "action" (*kriyā*), since even knowledge does not deviate from being of the nature of action. When that power, having withdrawn all its operations, abides in its own essential nature alone, Śiva becomes denotable by such terms as "the Powerful One" (*śakta*). That very [power] is his...
The state of dissolution of the presiding deity, whose nature is the supreme bindu, is now described. || 266 ||

Now, he says that in the state of enjoyment (bhoga), this [power] is denoted by such terms as "the exerted one" (udyuktā) and so forth: "That very [power], unfolding while languid from the weight of the seed-syllable (bindu) it has attained within its womb, intensely manifests for the Lord a continuous flow of supreme bliss. (267)
And that power (*śakti*), by means of exertion, brings about the tendency of the *bindu*—the effect—to be oriented toward production;

when it manifests the Lord’s (*pati*) continuous stream of supreme bliss and the perfection of knowledge and action through the generation of the effect, then that constitutes the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of Śiva, which consists of preservation. It is not, however, that Śiva possesses a supreme bliss or an excess of pleasure as his enjoyment.
It should be explained as being of the nature of the experience of bliss, because those two [qualities], being impure, cannot possibly exist in Śiva, who is by nature stainless. || 267 ||
At that time, he says that this [Lord], denoted by terms such as "the ever-exerted" (*udyukta*), shines forth together with that exerted power (*śakti*):

"That glorious Lord Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the five mantras, who is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), is eternally and constantly delighted by her, being ever-exerted. (268)

Therefore, the meaning is this: it is the very powers (*śakti*)—consisting of the five mantras beginning with Īśāna—which, though distinct due to their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of effects, perform the function of a body for Śiva; they are called His "body," but not in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*). As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*:

"That body [of Śiva] consists of the five mantras useful for the fivefold acts; through the mantras Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha, [the body's parts] from the head downwards are constituted."
(vi0 3|8-9) Therefore, it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara that the mention of its form in the scriptures is solely for the purpose of meditation:

"This form is traditionally taught for the sake of the practitioner's objective. And here, because the distinction between the states of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth of Śiva and Śakti is produced by the different stages of the *bindu*, and because that [state] is heard of as being the state of dissolution in the form of the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*).
