The locus of experience (*bhogādhiṣṭhāna*) consists of the transformation of the four *kalās*, beginning with *śānti*. It is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* that through this locus, the experience of even Śiva is proclaimed: "That which consists of the four forms, radiant, both *sakala* and *niṣkala*—in that, the experience of the Lord of the universe is always designated" (*Viṣamapada* 3.34). If this is so, [then...]

Since the Lord’s state of Sadāśiva consists precisely in presiding over the world of Sadāśiva, and since he alone is the embodiment of the five mantras, how can there be a mention of him here in the context of the state of enjoyment (*bhoga*)? It is stated thus because Śiva is to be meditated upon in the worlds of *nivṛtti* and so forth solely in the form of the mantras Sadyojāta and the others; [here, however,] he is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the five mantras.

He will state that the "form" (*mūrti*) of one who has entered the state of authority (*adhikārāvastha*) exists precisely in the world of Sadāśiva, beginning with the verse "That [arises] from the *bindu*" (verse 279). Furthermore, this matter is shown in detail in the venerable *Mataṅga*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. || 268 ||
Now he explains the nature of the mantra as power (śakti):

"Because it contemplates all states of being and protects from the ocean of saṃsāra, that power, whose nature is that [of the mantra], possesses the characteristics of contemplating and protecting. (269)

As it has been said: "Mentation (*manana*), omniscience (*sarvaveditva*), protection (*trāṇa*), and favor toward those in *saṃsāra*—because he possesses the nature of mentation and protection, he is designated as 'Mantra'.
And this etymological derivation applies equally to Śiva, to Śakti, and to the Lords of Knowledge (*Vidyeśvara*) and others; and therefore—
The term "mantra" is applied by way of metaphorical usage to words that denote [the deity]. || 269 ||
And he states that its differentiation is merely conditional (aupādhika):
"Due to the difference in effects and by virtue of her presiding over them, she, though one alone, appears fivefold;
she shines within the sphere of the five objects of her governance, beginning with Bindu and Śānti. (270)
It has already been stated previously that this [system] is divided into Īśāna and the others due to its presiding over the worlds beginning with Bindu and Śānti. He elaborates on this very point:
"Bindu, Śānti, Kalā, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti."
The places of enjoyment for these five are designated as "bindu" by Śiva. || 271 ||

Now, it might be objected: "Has it not been stated that the four worlds beginning with Śānti alone are the locus of enjoyment? True; however, although the Supreme Bindu, which consists of the state beyond Śānti, is of the nature of the state of dissolution (layāvasthā), its worlds arise precisely at the commencement of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
Therefore, there is no contradiction in stating that those [worlds] also constitute a locus of enjoyment here. || 271 ||
Therefore, because these *bindu-kalās* exist in the form of dissolution during their causal state, he calls them by the name "Supreme Bindu" (*parabindu*):
"This undivided state of the five *kalās* is designated as *bindu*.
That which pertains to it is the Supreme Form (*parā mūrti*); the other is the Lower [form] (*aparā*), which pertains to the realm of effects. (272)

The meaning is that the supreme form (parā mūrti) is the power (śakti) presiding over the bindu in the state of dissolution, whereas the non-supreme form (aparā mūrti) of Śiva is that which presides over the effects. || 272 ||
And thus:
"That stainless power of Śiva which is inherent (samavāyinī) is itself his form; due to the differentiation of its functions, it is called the body known as Sādākhya. (273)

The meaning is that the very power inherent in the transformation of the *bindu*, while exercising its *adhikāra* (sovereign authority) by presiding over the world of Sadāśiva— which lies below the worlds of the *nivṛtti*-kalā— is figuratively called the "body" (*tanu*) known as Sadāśiva. || 273 ||

It has been stated that while there is indeed a distinction among those who have attained various worlds through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and other means, the distinction between Śiva and Śakti—the two presiding deities—is due to the difference in their functions; thus he says:
"Mahāmāyā is presided over by the powerful Śiva."
For those who are established in the abode of enjoyment, who are stainless, and whose nature is Śiva; || 274 ||
That which produces the body, objects of enjoyment, the sense organs, the locus, consciousness, and so forth, is the effect;
that power of action is likewise called by that name. (275)

Whatever effect Mahāmāyā, agitated by Śiva and Śakti, produces, it receives the respective designation of those two—Śiva and Śakti—who preside over it; this occurs through metaphorical attribution based on the difference in the effects and the difference in their locations. For example, [it is so called] by virtue of presiding over the world of Śānti.
And when that [power] arises, even *śakti* is designated as *śānti*, and *śiva* is designated as *śānta*. This should be understood in other cases as well.

As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "But whatever distinction of Lords (*pati*) exists here in this scripture, like the distinction of powers (*śakti*), is due to the metaphorical application of the distinction of functions, and because of the distinction of their respective locations. (Vi. 13.164–165). || 274–275 ||
He elaborates on this very point: "Indeed, the power of the Wielder of the Trident is one, consisting of the forms of all knowledge and action;
for from it arise will, knowledge, action, and the rest, which are the sources of all effects. (276)

The states such as will, knowledge, and so forth, which have Him as their source and belong to Him, are the origins of effects; the meaning is that they are produced by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of effects. || 276 ||

Thus it has been stated that Śakti alone is the form (mūrti) of Śiva, having as its object his creative activity; now he says that for those residing in the principles (tattvas) pertaining to the qualification for enjoyment (bhoga-adhikāra), their bodies and so forth are likewise composed of the Bindu, just as previously described:
"And for the Īśvaras and the Śivas, [their forms] are likewise composed of Mahāmāyā."
The body, senses, and so forth are pure, auspicious, and possessed of their own respective functions. || 277 ||
But she who performs that [action]—this very power consisting of action (kriyātmikā) is inseparable from Śiva;
through connection with her, Śiva is said to be the cause of all effects. (278)
The state of authority (adhikārāvasthā) is now described:

Having descended from the Bindu and being surrounded by the individual souls (aṇu) and Sadāśiva, he [the Lord] [proceeds] through the offices of the duties of the Pati [to] Sadāśiva and Maheśvara. (279)
The Lord shines, sending forth [the powers] at the summit of the entire path.

Here, "causing to descend" (*avatāraṇa*) means being set in motion by abandoning the state of exertion (*udyoga-avasthā*); and this "setting in motion" refers to the Vidyeśvaras—who are Sadāśivas to be refined—respectively, regarding their enjoyment of their own worlds and their authority over the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*).
This is the application. For this very reason, being by nature capable of manifesting power and presiding over all paths, he shines forth in the form of Sadāśiva;
the meaning is that he becomes the object of meditation. || 279 ||
He shows that very basis for the form of the object of meditation:
"Śiva, the Lord, who has five streams as his mouth, is peaceful and has Śakti as his crest. (280)
His large eyes are vision, action, and will; he is endowed with the digit of the moon of consciousness;
his head is Īśāna, his face is the Puruṣa, and his circle of arms extends through the ten directions. || 281 ||
With the Aghora heart-mantra and the Vāma secret-mantra, this god has become manifest with a radiant body; he is active, possessed of all parts, and the purifier of all. || 282 ||
And here, by the term "five streams" (pañcasrotas), the five distinct states of the power whose nature consists of reflection (manana) and protection (trāṇa) are expressed. (280–282)
Having thus demonstrated the oneness of Śiva and Śakti despite the distinction in their presiding over the states of the bindu, he concludes:
"Śiva alone is one, and likewise Śakti is unchanging; for in the matters of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority, they both consist of pure consciousness alone. (283)
Now, in order to show that their multiplicity is merely figurative by means of another method, he states the actual difference between the selves (ātman) who partake of those respective states:
"For instance, in the stainless, vast, and deep great ocean of consciousness..."
They dissolve into their own self; therefore, some are established in meditative absorption (samādhi). || 284 ||

Some souls whose impurities have been fully transformed, being presided over by that Śiva as the bestower of grace and liberated by his power of grace, remain dissolved in their own self—their essential nature—which is like an ocean of exceedingly pure, unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence; the meaning is that through his grace, they attain liberation in the form of equality with him. However, they do not achieve oneness with the self of Śiva.

It should be explained that they "proceed," because non-duality has already been negated previously. And these [deities] are said to possess the state of dissolution (layāvasthābhāj) because they are equal to Śiva in the state of dissolution. || 284 ||

He states that even those who are "consciousness-alone" (vijñānakevalin) are said to abide in a state of dissolution because their impurity and māyā have not yet been transformed, because they rely upon mahāmāyā, because they are devoid of enjoyment, and because they are inactive: "Others, whose own powers are restrained by Śiva, lie dormant."
Regarding those who partake in the state of enjoyment (bhoga), he says: "Embracing Mahāmāyā, who possesses another mode of activity... (285).

The meaning is that those who are greedy for enjoyments and whose intellects are one-pointedly fixed on the pleasure of contact with that [Mahāmāyā] exist by resorting to Mahāmāyā, which has transformed itself into the form of the worlds beginning with Śānti. || 285 ||
The author, though himself possessing the authority [to speak], says further: "Likewise, others, having resorted to the supreme ether at the summit of the path... (286).

It has been stated that Ananta and the others, following the command of their Lord, perform the fivefold acts; by the command of Śiva, they abide in the worlds of Paravyoman and Mahāmāyā at the summit of the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan) and become performers of the fivefold acts. 286.
Then, even one among those who possess the authority over dissolution and enjoyment— || 287 ||
By virtue of being the presiding agent, power attains a figurative distinction; it is considered to be exactly like that [the Self]. Now, the difference between these two is stated. (288)
The mutual distinction between these two, Śiva and Śakti, is now described. || 287-288 ||
He states that very distinction:
"In the pure path, Śiva is the agent; Śakti is the dependent cause.
He should be known as their common substratum, consisting of his own dense, self-abiding consciousness. (289)
The distinction between these two is solely by way of being the property and the possessor of the property. || 289 ||

And in that regard, he says that while the nature of the subject (dharmin) is consciousness itself as established in its own being, that which consists in the capacity for grasping objects is spoken of as its attribute (dharma):
"But that [consciousness], arising with a craving to grasp all objects..."
And her majesty consists of supreme sovereignty, and its nature is pervasiveness. || 290 ||
And therefore—this Maheśvara is great, pervading all objects for those two;
because he possesses the power to pervade all objects, Śiva is the pervader of all objects. This has already been explained.
He clarifies this with the words "of those two" (tayor iti). || 290 ||
That consciousness which is independent of anything else is designated as Śiva. || 291 ||
The wise say that its power is a form dependent on another;
"dependent on another" means dependent on an object. || 291 ||
If it is asked, "Why is it postulated thus?", he says:
"Because there is the cognition of two aspects even for every single object. (292)
Power residing in Śiva exists through both dependence on another and independence.

This is because, in the case of an insentient object, the capacity of fire to burn is observed when it is in proximity to something combustible; otherwise, that capacity would not be manifested. And in the case of the sentient subject, namely the Self, there exists the nature of the grasper, which consists of the apprehension of objects and is established in itself.
The meaning is that this is established because it is proven by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, power exists. || 292 ||
If this is so, what is the distinction between this power of the self and the power of Śiva? To this he says:
"That [power] of the Lord, whose manifestation is eternally arisen and uninterrupted... (293).
With respect to the objects of knowledge, those to be presided over, and their effects, there is no further cause and so forth;
therefore, it is logical that the power of the Lord consists in a nature that is dependent upon another.

Since the Lord is eternally liberated, with respect to objects such as that which is to be known, He has no dependence on instruments such as the intellect apart from His own power (*śakti*), nor does He depend on auxiliary factors such as light. Therefore, for Him, power alone constitutes the nature of dependence on another, and nothing else.
For bound souls, however, this cause of effects and so forth is merely their own essential nature, which consists of power and depends upon objects.
[The opponent might argue: "It must be so, because we observe that for those things, there is a dependence on instruments and the like at the time of their production. To this he says:
"It cannot be the case that everything has a nature dependent on another, because effects such as a son and the like are perceived in quite a different way. (295)

Regarding the reading "of Śiva," the meaning is that the knowledge of the solitary Śambhu does not consist merely in abiding in his own essential nature; rather, it is necessarily dependent upon an object as the cause for its activity and so forth. This is because, in the case of bound souls who perceive effects such as sons, we observe that their arising of knowledge and the like occurs only through dependence on objects such as the father. || 295 ||
Therefore, he says that even for Īśvara, a cognition consisting of apprehension cannot be objectless:
"But a cognition without an object is not itself the apprehension of an object;
for if this were so, it would be observed that [cognition] arises only when an object is present."

Is there not the consequence that the very nature of phenomena (dharmasvarūpa) would be impermanent? No, for Śiva is always the object of perception as eternally existing entities such as the *bindu*, and because the capacity for apprehension, being inherent in the subject (*grahītṛ*), persists at all times.
[Objection: But surely, since we observe the sequential arising of the cognition of yellow and so forth following the destruction of the cognition of blue and so forth in individual selves (*ātman*)?
Is the impermanence of its capacity also indicated? To this he says: "Because of contradiction or because of succession; even so, that which is indestructible [is not]. (296)
This is the nature of perishable things: that at a given time, there is no arising of something else.

Because a mental cognition (*buddhi*) in the form of the determination of yellow—which is distinct from the form of the determination of blue and so forth—is perishable and mutually contradictory, even if it arises in succession, [there is] the incapacity for the apprehension of cognitions in the form of this or that pleasure and so forth.

Because it is always experienced as being inherent in the grasper, it is indeed imperishable; therefore, this transformation belongs only to the Buddhist [view], otherwise it would not be so. || 296 ||
And therefore:
"That which is indestructible is accepted as eternal; it is distinct from this [world]. (297)
Śakti exists by virtue of its locus in Śambhu, and He exists in her likewise.
Therefore, that too—the capacity of the Self—must be accepted as eternal, just like the capacity of Śiva.

And thus, although there is no difference in essence between Śiva and Śakti, there is indeed a real distinction between the substratum (dharmin) and its attribute (dharma); this he states with the word "asmāt" (from this). Therefore, for that reason.
Therefore, the meaning is that power is indeed of the very nature of phenomena (dharma). || 297 ||
Here, a further objection may be raised:
"Even in that which is a mass of consciousness, the designation 'power' (śakti) might indeed occur due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of effects. (298)
However, some maintain that power does not exist as a reality dependent upon another;
the meaning is that the nature of the substratum (dharmin) alone is the ultimate reality, and not the nature of its attributes (dharma). || 298 ||
To this, the reply is: one who performs an effect without an instrument would be an agent [in the literal sense]. || 299 ||
This opinion is indeed improper, as it is contradicted by both reasoning and perception.

For we observe that agents such as potters and others do not exercise agency without an instrument; therefore, since Śiva is also an agent, he must likewise possess some instrument. That [instrument] is none other than his own power (*śakti*). As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "And the instrument..."
"Power is not different [from the possessor of power]" (Vi. 3.4). Thus, it has been stated that for the selves as well, power alone is the instrument in bodily movement and so forth. || 299 ||
Furthermore, if the ultimate reality in the form of the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*) is not admitted,

then even during the state of persistence (*sthiti*), because there would be no apprehension of objects that are the effects of *bindu*— namely the categories beginning with Sadāśiva which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—

it would be illogical to postulate distinctions such as Sadāśiva and the rest for this [consciousness]. If, on the other hand, one were to admit the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of these distinctions even when the limiting adjuncts are not apprehended...
The state of authority would exist at all times, and not the state of dissolution, because there is no distinction [between them]; thus he says:
"Furthermore, even if the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is not grasped, it would still be the effect of the Lord. (300)

How could Śiva be free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi) if he were always possessed of such a state? Furthermore, if the *bindu* and other elements are not apprehended, then his agitation (*kṣobha*) and so forth would also be impossible, because an instrument cannot function for one who does not know it. Thus he says:
"Or how could he be an agent if he were devoid of knowledge of the instruments? (301)

Furthermore, since even the selves possess qualities equal to those of Śiva and are of the nature of a substratum (*dharmin*), it would be impossible for them to experience enjoyment in the form of the perception of pleasure and so forth if knowledge were not admitted as being of the nature of an attribute (*dharma*). Thus he says:
"Or else, how could the person perceive the intellect without that [intellectual] power?"
And this being so:
"This entire world would be blinding darkness, were it not for the lamp of power. (302)
Furthermore, what could the Blessed One do if he were powerless?
The meaning is that if power is not admitted, the world would become devoid of all activity for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
And therefore—
In the same way, the power of Śambhu is held to be non-different from him, yet it is conceived as distinct.

Just as a lentil (*masūra*) is not distinct from a thumb, even though they are said to be different for various reasons— just as a specific grain called a lentil, though belonging to the same genus as that which is called a thumb, is distinguished by some form or other— so too,

although there is no state of being separate entities between Śiva and Śakti, their distinction is established by way of the relationship between the substratum (*dharmin*) and its attribute (*dharma*). And in this regard:

Having accepted their identity on the basis of belonging to the same class (*samānajātīyatva*), the status of this as an illustration was stated; however, in reality, there is a difference between the thumb and the sun due to their distinctness. Thus, although Śiva and Śakti are different insofar as they stand in the relation of substratum and attribute (*dharmidharmatā*), there is no difference between them like that between two separate selves, because of their relationship of identity (*tādātmya*). He states this with the words: "Nor is it said to be different" (303).
Thus, although there is no internal difference between power and the possessor of power, having established their distinction by way of attribute and substratum, he concludes:
"Therefore, although non-different from Śambhu, that [power] is distinct as his inherent [attribute]. (304)
And its innate radiance is stainless, like that of the sun, rooted in that [power].
Now, one might ask: "Shiva will perform his work by means of the power called Bindu alone; what is the use of this [other power]? To this he says:
"For this Blessed Lord does not [act] by means of a power that is absolutely distinct from his own self. (305)
Sometimes he performs some action, yet he does not know anything at all.

Because the *bindu* is external and insentient by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna*), Śiva is unable—without his own inherent power (*śakti*) which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—to take objects such as the *bindu* and so forth as his domain, nor can he produce their agitation and the like; this applies even to a potter and others.
Because it is perceived precisely as being endowed with the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 305 ||

If this is so, since even the Lord would be incapable of acting without power (*śakti*), let that [power] alone be the cause of the world. As they say: "Salutations to you, without whom even the Omniscient One would not exist. This is not so; for since power is an attribute (*dharma*), it cannot exist without a substratum (*āśraya*). That very possessor of power (*śaktimān*), who is its substratum, is the creator of the universe by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*); thus he says:
Even though no distinction has been established, the cause is the god Maheśvara.
Now, regarding the metaphorical attribution of difference based on the power of the agent, he states the ultimate difference in effects which serves as the limiting condition:
"The difference in effects of an effect may also arise from a particular state. He elaborates upon this very point:
This *bindu*, its function dissolved, is impelled by Śiva and Śakti. || 307 ||
For the sake of creation, preservation, and the dissolution of the manifold world of the Creator, it is indeed the Bindu alone, having long established the universe, that proceeds [to act]. (308)
Just as clay, having reached a different state, begins to form a jar, so too does this [the self] previously undergo a transition into another state. (309)
Overpowered by the power of the Lord through various specific functions,
the wielder of the trident accomplishes diverse effects even though he is changeless.

Even though no transformation has occurred, [the seed] undergoes the states of division, drying, and powdering, which arise from the distinct stages occurring in the sequence previously described. || 311 ||
The Creator is like the lotus and the sun;
likewise, Śiva is the agent of the activities of creation and so forth, being both changeless and endowed with power.

If it is asked, "For what purpose does He perform the work of creation and so forth?", we reply: "It is for the sake of favoring bound souls (paśu). If this is so, then even though Śiva is the benefactor of all, why does He grant liberation to only some and not to everyone? If you say that this is simply His nature, then He would be internally possessed of attachment and aversion. To this, he says:
Just as the sun, though itself undergoing no change, is the cause of the melting of beeswax and the drying of clay in an instant, without requiring any external assistance. || 313 ||
Likewise, Śiva, though himself unchanging, brings about bondage and liberation for the atoms known as karma—whether equal or unequal, one's own, meritorious, or sinful. (314)
It is true that Śiva is the benefactor of all; yet in Him no passion or the like exists, because He is devoid of beginningless impurity (*anādimala*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that the agency of bondage and liberation belongs to the selves alone, due to their own fitness (*yogyatva*). Consequently, just as the sun, though uniform in form, by its mere proximity causes the liquefaction of beeswax—which is fit for melting—and the drying of clay—which is fit for desiccation—so too [does Śiva act].

And it causes dryness; likewise, Śiva also effects liberation for those whose impurities are matured and who are fit for liberation, while he effects bondage for those whose impurities are immature and who are fit for bondage, so that they may ripen—thus there is no contradiction. Therefore, in this context, by the term "merit and demerit"—he who is equanimous neither rejoices at a favor nor becomes angry at an injury.

"Among all beings, he is called one liberated while living"—according to this principle, two types of action consisting of benefit and harm are mentioned. When equanimity of mind arises through the ripening of those two, liberation occurs; in its absence, however, there is only bondage. But it is not the case that merit and demerit consist merely of the horse-sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin; rather, it is their equanimity [that matters].

It should be explained that [the equilibrium of karma] is the cause of liberation; otherwise, it would contradict the scriptures, because such an equilibrium of karma is possible even during the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), as its purpose is fulfilled merely by its own destruction. Furthermore, even the equilibrium of all karma is a cause only for the state of being a *vijñānakevalin*, and thus cannot possibly be the cause of liberation; rather, it is only the ripening of impurity (*mala*) that [is the cause].

Furthermore, because it is possible for that which is inferable from the signs of the equilibrium of the aforementioned karmas to become a cause of liberation through the gateway of initiation (*dīkṣā*), we have explained this in detail in our *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*. It has also been established by the Teachers in their commentaries on the *Śrīmat-Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*, the *Kiraṇatantra*, the *Mataṅgatantra*, and others; therefore, one should attend to those works. (313–314)
And for this reason:
"By the convergence of two karmas whose ripening has been obstructed through mutual contradiction, the power of Śiva descends upon the individual soul. (315)

When there is a conjunction of two actions of opposing results—such as dharma and adharma in the form of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), both having the fruit of heaven; or two forms of dharma having the fruit of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*); or two forms of adharma having the fruit of the Avīci and Raurava hells—the Śiva-power (*śakti*), which bestows the state of Śiva and is gracious, does not descend upon the self; for that [descent] depends solely upon the ripening of impurity (*mala*).
Because [the soul] falls due to hearing [the truth]. However, it is the power of obstruction itself that falls by means of *niyati* for the purpose of exhausting opposing karma.

As it is stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*: "In this ripening of merit and demerit... (*Viṣamapāda* 13.15), and so forth; thus, initiation alone—which is inseparable from the ripening of impurity—is the cause of liberation by way of the exhaustion of karma. As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*:

"Karma that would otherwise lead to many births is, like a burnt seed, obstructed by the subtle [powers]; for even that which was to come into being is restrained by him through experience. (6.19). Thus, when the impurity has reached maturity, there occurs the descent of the Graceful Power. 315.
As soon as that [mirror] has fallen [into his hand], he perceives himself with the dense veil shaken off, his impurities and turbidity stilled. || 316 ||
The meaning is that, through the removal of the veil of impurities, his nature—consisting of omniscience and so forth—is revealed when liberated from them. || 316 ||
For he is liberated at that very moment when, by the will of Śiva, he is touched by the power of Śiva known as initiation; once touched, he is indeed liberated.
And after the time of initiation, for the sake of destroying the bondage of the commenced effects,
he engages in the highest [state] through constant and occasional ritual action.
Even there—by means of this very body, the great-souled ones attain the supreme, unbroken pervasion; for these yogins of Śiva are indeed blessed. (318)
The meaning is that through the practice of yoga, omniscience and other such qualities are manifested right here [in this very state]. || 318 ||
In this context, he describes the greatness of the Śiva-yogi:
"He purifies, by his very play, rivers, countries, gardens, cities, and so forth, with his glance, his speech, his foot, and his hand. (319)
How much more so this person who has come for refuge and is terrified of worldly existence?
Now, the author of the treatise pays homage to his own guru:
"Salutations to our Guru, who is Śiva’s splendor in such a form. (320)
Regarding the question, "By whom was this treatise composed as a treasury of the jewels of yoga that bestow infinite fruits? he says here:
"By one whose mind has been purified by the *Āloka* composed by Rāmakaṇṭha. (321)
This *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā* was composed by Śrīkaṇṭha Sūri, who thus followed the excellent commentary of Śrī Rāmakaṇṭha;
the meaning of the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā* has been revealed here in brief. (322)
The Examination of the Three Jewels is completed.
By that lord of poets, there were composed the *Rasavān*, the *Āścaryasāra*, the *Pāṣaṇḍāpajaya*, the *Kāvyatilaka*, the *Bhaktaprakāśa*,
as well as the *Abhyudaya* among dramas, and the *Sadvṛttayaḥ* among Śaiva works, all with beautiful speech.
The *Ratnatrayollekhinī* has been well composed by Sthirāghoraśiva.
Thus ends the *Ratnatrayollekhinī*, composed by the teacher Aghoraśiva.
